news.title: '60 Minutes' opens 59th season on CBS with no direct mention of show's off-season turmoil
news.text:
The venerable newsmagazine “60 Minutes” opened its 59th season on CBS-TV on Sunday night with no direct mention of the turmoil and departures that have unfolded behind the scenes in recent months. 

Hosts waited until the show's end to acknowledge that anything different was going on. 

While speaking about the claim that there is a narrow window to make artificial intelligence safe for humanity, an announcer segued into the topics of journalism and “60 Minutes”: “For almost 60 years it has meant the same thing — journalism you can trust. Where we’re headed we’re going to need it,” the announcer said at the end of the show. 

He also noted that there were going to be “new faces” on the show this season.

CBS News leader Bari Weiss has said that the news show would take a “new approach.” That included firing the top producer and two correspondents, among others, and installing a new chief with no TV broadcast experience. One of the show’s most famous and enduring faces, Scott Pelley, was absent, fired after a tense confrontation with bosses earlier this year. 

Two other correspondents were dismissed and Anderson Cooper left of his own accord. 

Pelley has leveled unsettling accusations against the organization's leaders. “New management has instructed me to inject falsehoods and bias into a politically sensitive story,” the correspondent and former evening news anchor contended in June. CBS denied that.

Turmoil has been evident at “60 Minutes” for more than a year, after President Donald Trump sued the show over its editing of a 2024 interview with then-Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris. It became part of a broader upheaval at CBS News after Weiss was named to the new role of editor-in-chief by parent company Paramount late last year following the arrival of David Ellison as the network’s corporate leader.

Weiss appointed Nick Bilton, a former technology columnist and documentarian, as executive producer earlier this year, replacing Tanya Simon, a 30-year veteran of the show who’d been in the top job about a year. 

Also let go were correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi, whose segment about Trump administration deportees in a Salvadoran prison was abruptly pulled by Weiss before running a month later, and Cecilia Vega.
news.summary: The venerable newsmagazine “60 Minutes” opened its 59th season on CBS-TV on Sunday night

news.title: 2026 midterm election races to watch
news.text: CBS News' Battleground Tracker polling is back for 2026, capturing what's on voters' minds and the key groups to watch coast to coast, as well as what it means for districts, seat estimates and control of the U.S. House of Representatives.Every district and state matters, but CBS News also identifies nine key Senate and 42 House races that will likely decide the majority — all of which can change as the campaign rolls on.Democrats and Republicans are focusing on a small number of races in the House and the Senate as they fight for control of Congress in the midterm elections this fall.Republicans, who currently have the majority in both chambers, are vulnerable primarily because of the unpopular Iran war and continuing cost-of-living economic pressure. SenateRepublicans have 53 seats, and Democrats have 47. Most of the 22 seats the GOP is defending are in states Mr. Trump easily won in 2024. Democrats must add a net total of four seats to take the majority while also defending a few seats against GOP challenges.Here are the nine 2026 Senate races to watch:AlaskaGOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola are the front-runners in Alaska's top-four primary, where another candidate by the same name as the incumbent is also on the ballot. Alaska hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008, but the party is eyeing the race as a pickup opportunity.IowaGOP Rep. Ashley Hinson and state Rep. Josh Turek are facing off in Iowa after Sen. Joni Ernst decided not to seek reelection. The race has grown surprisingly competitive in a state that's shifted to the right in recent years, as affordability issues and the Trump tariff policies weigh on Iowans.MaineGOP Sen. Susan Collins is defending her seat against Troy Jackson, who became the Democratic nominee after Graham Platner bowed out of the race in July following a sexual assault allegation. Collins has survived challenges in previous reelection fights, but Democrats are optimistic about their chances in a state that Kamala Harris won in 2024 by almost 7 points.MichiganFormer GOP Rep. Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed are vying for an open seat in Michigan after Sen. Gary Peters decided to retire from Congress. El-Sayed is a progressive former Michigan health official who defeated a more moderate opponent in a divisive Democratic primary, while Rogers is seeking the seat after losing a bid to Sen. Elissa Slotkin last cycle. OhioGOP Sen. Jon Husted is defending his seat against a comeback bid by former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost his reelection bid in Ohio's other Senate seat last cycle. Democrats are hoping Brown's working-class brand will propel him to victory against Husted, the former lieutenant governor who was appointed to JD Vance's seat last year after Vance became vice president. TexasTexas Attorney General Ken Paxton and state Rep. James Talarico are competing in a closely watched contest in the Lone Star State. Democrats saw their chances of flipping the seat improve after Paxton defeated incumbent GOP Sen. John Cornyn, given Paxton's history of personal controversies and more conservative positions. But Republicans remain confident in their chances of holding onto the seat, though some concede that the race will be tough — and expensive.GeorgiaGOP Rep. Mike Collins is taking on Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia in a competitive race that was once expected to be the easiest pickup opportunity for Republicans. But a messy Republican primary slowed the launch of Republicans' general election fight to unseat the first-term senator.North CarolinaFormer Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper and former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley are jockeying for a seat representing North Carolina in the Senate after GOP Sen. Thom Tillis announced he wouldn't seek reelection. Democrats see the seat in the Tar Heel State as a key prize, representing their best chance at flipping a seat this cycle.New HampshireDemocratic Rep. Chris Pappas and former GOP Sen. John Sununu are running for an open Senate seat in New Hampshire to fill Sen. Jeanne Shaheen's seat upon her retirement. New Hampshire hasn't elected a Republican to the Senate since 2010, but Republicans are hopeful about the prospects for Sununu, whose family has been dominant in Granite State politics.HouseAll 435 House seats are up for election, with 218 as the threshold for the majority. The House is currently very narrowly divided, with 218 Republicans, plus an independent who caucuses with the GOP, and 214 Democrats. Two seats are vacant.These are the 42 House races to watch:Arizona's 1st Congressional District Republican Jay Feely and Democrat Amish Shah are vying to replace eight-term GOP Rep. David Schweikert, who ran unsuccessfully for governor. Feely, an NFL veteran and former analyst for CBS Sports, initially ran in another district, but he switched at the urging of President Trump. Shah failed to unseat Schweikert in 2024. Arizona's 6th Congressional District Republican Rep. Juan Ciscomani is up against Marine veteran JoAnna Mendoza in the district that stretches from the Tucson-area suburbs down to the southeastern corner of the state along the U.S.-Mexico border. California's 13th Congressional District The seat held by Democratic Rep. Adam Gray is one of the House Republicans' campaign arm's top targets. Gray flipped the seat in 2024, narrowly winning by fewer than 200 votes. In 2022, he lost by fewer than 600 votes. In June's nonpartisan primary, he had a significant advantage over Republican Kevin Lincoln, a Marine veteran.California's 22nd Congressional District GOP Rep. David Valadao is one of two remaining House Republicans in Congress who voted to impeach President Trump in 2021 over the Capitol riot. He is the last one running for reelection, since Washington Rep. Dan Newhouse is retiring. Valadao is running against Democrat Randy Villegas in the newly redrawn district. California's 45th Congressional District Democratic Rep. Derek Tran's district was redrawn as part of Gov. Republican state Rep. Jennifer Balkom replaced Edwards on the ballot and will face Democrat Jamie Ager. news.title: Vulnerable House Republicans embrace Trump as GOP bets on defying midterm history
news.text: DALLAS — President Donald Trump is getting a much warmer reception from his fellow Republicans during this election cycle than his predecessor did from Democrats this time two years ago. Conventional political wisdom dictates that the party in power will suffer losses in Congress during a midterm election year. Americans who oppose the president's party are typically more motivated to vote than people who support their agenda. But the GOP is banking on the opposite effect. The first-ever GOP midterm convention featured back-to-back keynote addresses from the commander-in-chief, as well as speeches from his Cabinet officials, allies and members of Congress. "I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot," Trump told his audience on Wednesday. Republican incumbents and candidates running in battleground districts this November also took the stage, and all speakers projected confidence despite Trump's own low approval numbers. DEMOCRATS TARGETING 12 ADDITIONAL RED DISTRICTS IN MIDTERMS PUSH TO RETAKE HOUSE "We ran together in 2024 on a ticket with President Trump, [Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa.] and myself — voters elected all of us to deliver real change and results, and we've actually been able to do that with securing the border and delivering historic tax relief," Rep. Ryan Mackenzie, R-Pa., told Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the convention. "Now what we're seeing is in a midterm, we are actually going to defy the historic trends. Why is that? Because the Democrats are so far left they are totally out of touch." Republicans believe their warnings of Democrats' socialist insurgency will help them keep their majorities in the House and Senate this year, along with touting Trump's signature tax cuts in the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act. HOW ONE NYC SUBURB COULD DECIDE WHICH PARTY CONTROLS THE HOUSE Mackenzie is one of Democrats' top targets in the election cycle, along with Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., in the suburbs outside New York City. "He's the President of the United States, and whether it was Joe Biden or Donald Trump, I've always shown up," Lawler told Fox News Digital. "You have to be able to engage with the president, and, you know, frankly, this is where I think the Democrats have made a very big mistake. They could get a lot more in terms of what it is that they want if they would actually engage constructively." Lawler, Mackenzie and Rep. Rob Bresnahan, R-Pa., are the three vulnerable incumbents who took the stage during the convention last week. TRUMP HITS KEY BATTLEGROUNDS TO SELL TAX CUTS, BOOST GOP AHEAD OF MIDTERMS Lawler, for his part, introduced two residents from his district whose daughter was killed by an illegal immigrant in Chicago — a poignant symbol of what Republicans say could happen more often if Democrats win. Trump has also campaigned in each of their districts in recent months as he crisscrosses the country in a bid to keep control of Congress for the latter half of his final term. But it was not just vulnerable incumbents who appeared in Dallas alongside Trump. The two-day affair also brought candidates from across the country, even those running in tight races. GOP FACES BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS AS REPUBLICANS PAINT ELECTION AS ‘COMPETITION WITH COMMUNISM’ "When people say that folks are running away from President Trump, I'll tell you I'm certainly not doing that. And let me tell you why: because he has made promises to South Texas, and he has kept them, especially when we look at border security," candidate Eric Flores told Fox News Digital. JOHNSON DOWNPLAYS GOP'S MIDTERM WOES AS DEMOCRATS EYE HOUSE TAKEOVER: 'I AM VERY BULLISH' "My opponent, who said, you know, that the sleepy Joe Biden administration and the no-show border czar, Kamala Harris, were on the right track. Let me tell you firsthand, I was on Operation Guardian support, was a federal prosecutor on the border. It was a humanitarian crisis. President Trump, on day one, secured our border." Flores is running in a South Texas district currently represented by Rep. Vicente Gonzalez, D-Texas. Time will tell if the strategy pays off, but Democrats are already seizing on it in hopes that associating with Trump will sink GOP candidates like it did in 2018. TRUMP'S APPROVAL RATING PLUMMETS TO NEW LOW AHEAD OF CRITICAL MIDTERMS: 'MORE WORK TO DO' "Ryan Mackenzie, Rob Bresnahan and Scott Perry made their priorities clear tonight: they care more about Donald Trump’s cost-raising agenda than what’s best for the people of Pennsylvania," Pennsylvania Democratic Party Chair Eugene DePasquale said in a statement. "After jetting all the way to Texas to champion an agenda of higher gas prices, cost-raising tariffs, and healthcare cuts, Mackenzie, Bresnahan, Perry and the entire PA GOP have proven that they’ll put Trump ahead of our Commonwealth every single time — and Pennsylvanians are ready to send them packing this November." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital did not see Rep. Scott Perry, R-Pa., who is also expected to run a close race, at the convention, but reached out to his campaign for comment.
news.summary: President Donald Trump urged Republicans to "pretend that I'm on the ballot," as vulnerable GOP incumbents rallied at the first-ever midterm convention.
news.author: Elizabeth Elkind,Paul Steinhauser

news.title: ‘60 Minutes’ has survived setbacks and scandals before — but maybe not like this
news.text:
In “Mike Wallace is Here,” a worthwhile documentary currently playing on Netflix, Wallace’s biggest claim to fame “60 Minutes” is said to owe its success and staying power to its “hero journalists and sweating villains.”

Illustrating the point, the documentary includes a sequence in which Wallace confronts a nefarious-looking character in his office in the show’s trademark style, only to have the man initially seem delighted to meet the correspondent, recognizing him from TV, and somehow momentarily ignoring the implications of having Wallace and a camera crew on the other side of his desk.

Network television hasn’t been that big in a long time, and it probably never will be again. 

Network television hasn’t been that big in a long time, and it probably never will be again. But as one of the few things that has continued to work and reliably draw a large audience, “60 Minutes” remained a true institution, making CBS News’ decision to mess with its formula puzzling, aggravating and thanks to its corporate management team, politically suspect.

That’s the awkward background as the curtain rises on the television newsmagazine’s 59th season on Sept. 13 after months of principled departures, firings and enough public drama to turn the media newsletter industry into an ongoing soap opera. It’s just that the “sweating villains” in this scenario are Paramount CEO David Ellison and his hand-picked CBS News chief, Bari Weiss, fueling suspicions that they have tarnished the division’s “crown jewel” to mollify President Donald Trump and serve an agenda based on corporate priorities and ideology, not the high-minded journalism for which the program is known.

The premiere episode thus finds itself under a microscope, although frankly, first likely impressions won’t say much about the bigger picture. With the departure of correspondents Scott Pelley — who was fired after criticizing his bosses in June — Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega, one key question will be how the program fills its story pipeline in the coming weeks, given the time and industry historically involved in reporting and producing them.

For now, “60 Minutes” returns staffed with new faces and under the stewardship of two television novices: Weiss, whom Ellison installed after buying her right-leaning website, The Free Press; and her appointed executive producer, Nick Bilton. And if they have cobbled together a credible lineup — kicking off with, among other things, a profile of the Los Angeles Rams to capitalize on the NFL’s might as a lead-in — the fact that the Super Bowl favorite just lost its opening game in Australia underscores that in television, even what looks like a no-brainer isn’t necessarily a sure thing.

The larger issue is whether “60 Minutes” will sustain the qualities that defined it amid allegations of Weiss’ meddling and editorial interference — including charges of inserting White House “talking points” into stories — breaking from the independence the show’s success commanded. Plus, there’s the shadow of Paramount as it seeks to preserve its planned $110-billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery after the studio settled a frivolous lawsuit last year brought by Trump over a Kamala Harris profile during the 2024 presidential campaign.

Granted, “60 Minutes” has survived setbacks and scandals before. Speed bumps on its long journey have included caving to fears of the tobacco industry in 1995 to avoid a lawsuit as its corporate parent planned to merge with Westinghouse (a tale documented in the movie “The Insider”); and Dan Rather’s 2004 “60 Minutes II” report about then-President George W. Bush’s National Guard service — one of the stains conservatives regularly cite when accusing the program (and indeed, mainstream media in general) of the liberal bias they see under every nook and cranny.

Nevertheless, the newsmagazine has endured, marked by enviable stability preserving its ethos while passing the baton to new producers and talent. That includes veteran correspondents Lesley Stahl, 84, and Bill Whitaker, 75, who chose to stay despite public soul-searching following Pelley’s acrimonious exit, maintaining a link, however tenuous, to its storied past.

In “Mike Wallace is Here,” “60 Minutes” creator Don Hewitt admits to some bewilderment over why the show’s magazine format worked so well on television.

“This thing took off for reasons I still do not understand,” Hewitt said.

Part of the answer, of course, is that the show wasn’t just news, but great television, generating drama in a way that brought the medium to life — and, thanks to its commercial power, launched a thousand imitators, for better and often worse.

Yet while Hewitt, Wallace and their brethren didn’t immediately grasp what made “60 Minutes” tick, if a series that seemed like it would always be there begins slumping toward oblivion, no one will need to launch a major investigation this time to identify the culprits.
news.author: Allison Detzel

news.title: Donald Trump’s Approval Rating Shifts With America’s Most Educated
news.text: President Donald Trump’s approval rating among college-educated Americans has fallen sharply in recent weeks, potentially adding to Republicans’ challenges as they fight to retain control of Congress in November. Trump’s approval among college graduates fell from 34 percent in an Economist/YouGov poll conducted August 21-24 to 31 percent in its August 28-31 survey. It dropped again to 30 percent in the poll conducted September 4-8. Over the same period, disapproval rose from 63 percent to 69 percent, widening Trump’s net deficit with the group from 29 points to 39 points. The shift is politically significant because college graduates have become an increasingly important part of the Democratic coalition, while Trump’s 2024 victory was powered more heavily by voters without four-year degrees. About two-thirds of Trump’s voters did not have a college degree, according to a Pew Research Center analysis of validated voters. By contrast, college graduates accounted for 48 percent of former Vice President Kamala Harris’ supporters. The surveys do not establish what caused the decline but three consecutive readings in the same direction could be an ominous signal for Republican candidates whose races could be shaped by dissatisfaction with the president and turnout among college-educated voters. Polls have been known to underestimate Trump's popularity, with the president outperforming preelection expectations in three presidential campaigns. Speaking about the shift in Trump's general approval rating, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle previously told Newsweek: "The ultimate poll was November 5, 2024, when nearly 80 million Americans overwhelmingly elected President Trump to deliver on his popular and commonsense agenda. Newsweek has contacted the White House, via email outside of normal working hours, for comment. What the Polls Show The decline was driven not only by fewer college graduates approving of Trump’s performance, but also by an increase in the intensity of opposition to him. In the August 21-24 Economist/YouGov poll, 34 percent of college graduates approved of Trump’s job performance and 63 percent disapproved. Fifty-four percent said they strongly disapproved. The survey questioned 1,536 U.S. adult citizens, including 504 college graduates. One week later, Trump’s approval among college graduates fell to 31 percent, while disapproval increased to 68 percent. The proportion who strongly disapproved rose to 57 percent. That poll surveyed 1,592 adult citizens, including 563 college graduates. The September 4-8 poll recorded another, smaller shift: 30 percent of college graduates approved of Trump and 69 percent disapproved, including 61 percent who strongly disapproved. By comparison, 41 percent of respondents without a degree approved and 57 percent disapproved—giving Trump an 11-point approval advantage among Americans without college degrees. Trump also underperformed with college graduates on the issues tested in the latest survey. Among the group, 28 percent approved of his handling of the economy and 72 percent disapproved. His rating on inflation was lower still, with 25 percent approving and 73 percent disapproving. College graduates also gave him net-negative ratings on taxes and government spending. The polls’ overall margins of error ranged from approximately 3.4 to 3.5 percentage points. YouGov did not publish separate margins of error for college graduates, meaning week-to-week movement within the subgroup may fall within normal polling variation. Nevertheless, the three consecutive surveys show Trump moving in the same direction, with his net rating among college graduates deteriorating by 10 points in less than three weeks. What It Could Mean for the Midterms The same polls indicate that college graduates are currently leaning heavily toward Democratic congressional candidates. In the September 4-8 survey, 57 percent of college graduates said they planned to vote for the Democratic candidate in their district, compared with 28 percent who chose the Republican—a 29-point Democratic advantage. Among voters without degrees, Republicans led by 39 percent to 33 percent. The demographic could also be strongly represented at the polls: 78 percent of college graduates said they would definitely vote in November, compared with 67 percent of Americans without degrees. The findings suggest a Democratic advantage among college graduates, but national polling cannot predict individual congressional races, where local issues, candidates and turnout will help determine the results. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Ben Kelly and Robert Greenall
news.summary: Trump’s support among college graduates has declined as the voting bloc prepares to cast midterm ballots.

news.title: Elon Musk's PAC Spends $100 Million on Ads Attacking Democrats Over Transgender Policy in Midterms 2026
news.text: Elon Musk's political action committee, America PAC, has launched a multimillion-dollar advertising campaign centered on transgender policy issues, targeting Democratic Senate candidates in several competitive midterm races this fall.According to reporting from The New York Times, Musk has authorized the PAC to spend more than $100 million during the current election cycle, with an initial wave of ads focused heavily on transgender rights running across television, digital platforms and streaming services. The campaign marks the first large-scale, trans-focused advertising push of the 2026 midterm cycle from a major Republican-aligned outside group, according to AdImpact, a firm that tracks political advertising spending.Which races are being targetedThe ads have targeted Democratic candidates in four competitive Senate races: Rep. James Talarico in Texas, Sen. Sherrod Brown in Ohio, state Rep. Josh Turek in Iowa, and former Rep. Mary Peltola in Alaska. Additional ads have also targeted Michigan candidate Abdul El-Sayed, according to reporting from Truthout and Erin in the Morning, a newsletter focused on transgender policy coverage. America PAC has also placed some advertising in New Hampshire and Maine, though those ads reportedly did not focus on transgender issues.The advertisements vary by candidate but generally center on claims about gender-affirming care, transgender participation in sports, and related cultural themes. One ad targeting Turek states that he "voted to spend our tax dollars on sex change surgeries for children" and "voted to let biological men enter girls' locker rooms and bathrooms," according to a copy of the ad shared by AdImpact Politics. Other ads have made similar claims about the remaining candidates, addressing topics such as school bathroom policy and transgender athletes in women's sports.A shift in campaign strategyAxios reporter Mike Zapler noted that the emphasis on transgender issues represents a departure from the broader pattern of Republican Senate advertising so far this cycle. According to AdImpact's tracking data, transgender-focused messaging had been a comparatively minor theme in GOP Senate ads prior to America PAC's rollout.The strategic emphasis comes despite polling that generally shows economic concerns, rather than transgender policy, as the dominant issue for voters heading into the midterms. Zapler noted that Republican strategists appear to be drawing on the perceived effectiveness of similar messaging used during the 2024 presidential campaign, when advertising focused on transgender issues was widely credited with damaging Kamala Harris' presidential bid.Some of the targeted candidates have already shifted their public positions on related policy questions ahead of the ad campaign. Turek's campaign has issued statements opposing transgender women's participation in women's sports and opposing what his campaign described as "taxpayer-funded sex changes." Brown, in his 2024 campaign, also ran advertising referencing transgender athletes, including swimmer Lia Thomas, an approach some observers characterized at the time as an attempt to neutralize similar attacks from Republican opponents.Responses from targeted campaignsRepresentatives for some of the targeted candidates have pushed back publicly on America PAC's advertising campaign. A spokesperson for El-Sayed's Senate campaign in Michigan, Cole Wozniak, addressed Musk's spending directly in a statement to local press."It's no surprise that the world's first trillionaire would be trying to buy a Senate seat," Wozniak said.Wozniak also indicated that the campaign intends to keep its focus elsewhere rather than engaging directly on the transgender policy attacks. "Michiganders will see right through this," Wozniak said, "and will send Abdul to the Senate this November to take on the corruption by getting money out of politics, putting money in your pocket, and passing Medicare for All."El-Sayed separately drew public attention last month for declining to engage when Fox News host Jesse Watters pressed him on transgender rights during a televised interview, a moment that some commentators compared to the political approach taken by New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani in similar media appearances.Musk's history on transgender issuesMusk's involvement in transgender-focused political advertising predates the current cycle. A Reuters investigation previously found that Musk contributed $50 million to a far-right political action committee called Citizens for Sanity in 2022, a group with ties to former Trump adviser Stephen Miller that ran a series of ads focused on transgender-related topics in that cycle's competitive races.Musk has also spoken publicly and personally about transgender issues in the context of his own family. His daughter, model Vivian Wilson, came out as transgender in 2020. Musk has since made public comments critical of that decision, at one point saying she "was killed by the woke mind virus" and adding, "Now, the woke mind virus will die."Broader political contextThe advertising blitz arrives as Republicans face what political analysts have broadly described as a challenging midterm environment, with voters across the political spectrum expressing frustration over economic conditions, including elevated gas prices tied in part to the conflict involving Iran. Some conservative commentators have framed America PAC's strategy as an effort to mobilize base voters around cultural issues even in an environment where economic concerns dominate broader public polling.Conservative strategist Terry Schilling of the American Principles Project has previously described attacks centered on transgender participation in women's sports as a deliberate entry point for broader political messaging on transgender issues, telling CNN in earlier remarks that such messaging helped make "opponents of the LGBT movement comfortable with talking about transgender issues" more broadly.With America PAC's advertising campaign still in its early stages and additional spending expected as the November midterms approach, transgender policy is likely to remain a prominent flashpoint in several of the cycle's most competitive Senate races. Whether the strategy proves effective will likely depend on how voters in these individual states weigh the issue against other concerns, including the economy, as Election Day draws closer.
news.summary: Elon Musk's America PAC is spending tens of millions of dollars on transgender policy ads targeting Democratic Senate candidates in several competitive 2026 midterm races.

news.title: The six races that could lose Trump the Senate - and three he could win
news.text:
The Trump administration is looking at a bruising set of midterm elections that could result in the Republicans losing control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

Most analysts say that the Democrats are likely to gain control of the House because the Republicans only have a majority of four seats. However, to flip the Senate, the Democrats would need to retain all their seats and win four from the Republicans.

The Republicans, who were previously confident in their ability to keep the Senate, are struggling beneath the weight of Donald Trump’s unpopularity. Voters are increasingly dissatisfied with the US President’s decisions, high inflation, gas prices, the war on Iran and immigration among top concerns. 

And with less than two months to go until the 3 November elections, Democrats have been eyeing up states that once seemed beyond their reach, with Republicans increasingly unsure they can hang on to the 100-seat Senate.

Here are the nine standout races to watch that could determine control of the US Senate – six currently held by Republicans and three by Democrats. 

Democrats have been targeting Republican-held Maine, where incumbent Susan Collins has held her Senate seat since 1997 – despite the state leaning Democrat in presidential elections.

“On paper, Maine should be a comfortable win for the Democrats,” according to Nathan Gonzales of Inside Elections, a non-partisan political analysis organisation. Former vice president Kamala Harris won the state by 7 percentage points in 2024. 

However, “Susan Collins is tough to beat”, he added.

Dr Peter Finn, a lecturer in International Relations at the University of Greenwich, who curates the LSE United States Politics and Policy blog series on the midterms, told The i Paper that Collins could be a tricky opponent because she “is an independent within the Republican Party, she’ll go against the leadership if she thinks she should”. 

That means that voters dissatisfied with Trump might still vote to keep her on as senator.

The Democrats have already harmed their own campaign in Maine by their initial choice of candidate, Graham Platner. A progressive, an oyster farmer and ex-Marine, Platner attracted controversy over a tattoo that resembled a Nazi symbol, and ultimately had to drop out of the race due to allegations of sexual assault.

The current candidate is Troy Jackson, a former lumberjack and state legislator who shares Platner’s progressive politics. 

Recent polls show Jackson with a three- to four-percentage-point lead.

A traditionally Republican stronghold that has not seen a Democratic candidate win either of its Senate seats since 1993, Texas has become competitive.

Democrat candidate James Talarico, a former teacher and member of the Texas House of Representatives is close in the race against scandal-hit Republican Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general.

Dr Finn told The i Paper that the demographics of the state had changed in a way that was favourable to the Democrats. “It’s much more diverse than it was in the past, as with lots of places. I’m not saying it’s definitely going to happen. The cities lean Democrat and the bigger they become the more likely [a Democrat victory is],” he said.

The Democrats’ chances in Texas have been helped by the Republicans’ choice of candidate. Paxton is a Trump loyalist and a stalwart of Texas politics with a long history of scandal including multiple accusations of fraud and a failed attempt to overturn the 2020 presidential election by suing states that Joe Biden won. Last year his wife filed for divorce “on biblical grounds” over alleged infidelity, damaging Paxton’s conservative crusader image.

Paxton had to fight a vicious primary, in which he and his opponent John Cornyn tore metaphorical chunks out of each other and spent millions of dollars. A Trump-backed group has pledged to spend $10m in support of Paxton.

Kyle Kondik of the non-partisan analyst organisation Sabato’s Crystal Ball, told The i Paper that the organisation considered Texas a toss-up, rather than a sure thing for the Republicans, because: “The question is whether Paxton is too toxic to win even in a Republican state.”

In Ohio, former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown, a pro-trade union progressive, is going up against incumbent Jon Husted, who took Vice President JD Vance’s place in 2025 when he quit to serve as Vice President.

Non-partisan analysts such as the Cook Political Report, Inside Elections and Sabato’s Crystal Ball, have Ohio pegged as a toss-up despite the fact that the state has leaned towards the Republicans in recent years.

Recent polls show ​Brown leading Husted by three to four percentage points.

One factor in the race has been the unpopularity of data centres. Brown, who has a reputation for economic populism, has made data centres a focal point of his campaign, accusing his opponent of “being the face of data centres”.

The attacks appear to be resonating with voters. In a memo, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned that Brown’s messaging on data centres was “significantly more effective than traditional messaging” and described data centres as an “anchor hanging around Husted’s neck”.

Economic disillusionment over Trump’s tariffs and the rising cost of fuel and fertiliser in the agricultural state of Iowa mean the Republicans are at real risk of losing the state.

Democratic candidate Josh Turek is facing Ashley Hinson, who is fighting for the Republicans after the retirement of ⁠incumbent senator Joni Ernst.

Turek has campaigned hard in rural areas, targeting small farmers in his messaging and linking the cost of living crisis to Trump’ s war on Iran, and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. In a statement following Hinson’s vote to continue the war, he said: “By voting to continue this war in Iran, Ashley Hinson has once again shown that she does not care about Iowans. As gas prices hit nearly $4 per gallon and our farmers deal with skyrocketing input prices”.

According to the non-partisan analysts, the polling suggests that the state still leans Republican. However, the cost of living crisis for farmers has rendered the race much more competitive for the Democrats than would have previously been the case, and analysts say it may be one of the most competitive contests.

North Carolina

Democrats have a good chance to win North Carolina, where incumbent Republican senator Thom Tillis, an outspoken Trump critic, is retiring.

The Democratic candidate, former governor Roy Cooper, is well liked in the state. He was elected twice as governor in 2016 and 2020, even when Trump won the state in those presidential elections. 

Conversely, the Republican candidate, Michael Whatley, a Trump ally, has never previously run for office, and is likely to be damaged by his close association with the unpopular president.

Opinion polls show Cooper holding a steady lead over Whatley, who most recently chaired the Republican National Committee.

According to Nathan Gonzales from Inside Elections, “North Carolina is the Democrats’ best takeover opportunity”. 

Alaska, sometimes referred to as the “last frontier” has an unconventional voting system that puts the Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, in with a shot of taking the seat off Republican Senator Dan Sullivan.

Kyle Kondik of Sabato’s Crystal Ball said: “The ballot in Alaska Senate — 3 Rs vs. 1 D — is helpful to Peltola in that state’s unique top-four, ranked-choice system” because Republican votes may end up split.

Sullivan may also struggle with the fact that another of the candidates on the ballot is an independent called Dan J Sullivan, which the Republican candidate fears could result in confusion for voters, reducing his chances.

Peltola previously held the state’s one House seat for a single term and has campaigned as a centrist. in the nonpartisan primary last month she won 82,000 votes to Sullivan’s 69,000.

Alaska is another state in which the war on Iran and the attendant rise in the price of fuel has played into the race. The state is particularly vulnerable to hikes in the price of fuel because of the dispersed population and lack of roads. There is also a shortage in petrol and diesel power for off-grid generators used for electricity in remote areas, as well as off-road vehicles. Peltola has blamed the war on Iran for the rising costs.

However, the Democrats have weaknesses too, with three states they fear could be lost to the Republicans, reducing their chances of winning the Senate.

Democrats are hoping to keep their seat held by retiring senator Gary Peters. 

After a bloody primary in Michigan, progressive Abdul El Sayed won the Democratic nomination. He has since faced criticism from within the Democratic Party for his outspoken stance on Israel, and his association with the controversial streamer Hassan Piker. Centrist argue that he has taken left-wing stances unpopular with the Michigan electorate.

“Michigan will not only be a vital race because losing it would mean that the path to a Senate majority becomes significantly more difficult, but it is the only race where a candidate from the progressive wing is running in a swing seat,” said a source familiar with the campaign.

Losing Michigan might be taken as a signal of “how unelectable progressives are, dampening the hopes of the progressive wing of the party for getting the presidential nominee in 2028”. 

The source added that they thought El Sayed could still win in Michigan because its “overall polling shows such a strong lead for Democrats”.

In Georgia, the Democratic senator Jon Ossoff is up against Trump-backed Republican representative Mike Collins. Most polls show Ossoff leading.

That may, in part, be down to Ossoff’s acidic takedowns of Trump. The 39-year-old’s viral attacks appear to have dramatically helped his fundraising efforts. As The i Paper previously reported, in the second quarter of 2026 Ossoff raised $20m (£14.7m) and had $42m (£31m) on hand. In comparison, Collins had raised $2.1m (£1.5m) and had about $2m (£1.4m) on hand, giving Ossoff a 20 to one fundraising advantage. 

Ossoff’s youth and good looks have also led many to compare him to former president Barack Obama, and there is now growing interest among Democrats in an Ossoff 2028 presidential run.

Meanwhile Collins is facing scrutiny over reports that his former aide, Preson Parra, shared images of himself in Ku Klux Klan robes. Meyer Siegfried, a spokesperson for Collins, said: “Parra has no affiliation with Mike Collins’ office or campaign. The posts are vile, completely unhinged, and Mike Collins unequivocally condemns them.”

New Hampshire

New Hampshire is set to be crucial to the fight for the Senate majority.

John Sununu, who served in the Senate from 2003 to 2009, last week won the Republican nomination in New Hampshire. He will take on Chris Pappas, who was first elected to the House in 2018. They will be competing for the seat held by retiring Democratic senator Jeanne Shaheen. 

Non-partisan analysts say Democrats are leading but Republicans see New Hampshire’s open-seat status as one of their few opportunities to gain an advantage.

They also believe they have a strong candidate in Sununu. He comes from a well-known political family, as the brother of Chris Sununu, who was New Hampshire’s governor for eight years. His father is John H Sununu, who was chief of staff to President Bush. Trump gave his support to Sununu this year, despite a 2024 op‑ed in which Sununu called Trump a “loser”.

Speaking about the midterm elections generally Gonzales said: “Most of the close races will be determined by whether Trump-first Republican voters turn out in an election where he isn’t on the ballot and whether independent voters are most concerned about the current direction of the country under Republican control or the future direction of the country with Democrats in power.”

news.title: Alleged trespasser stopped by security at Kamala Harris' Malibu home: Sheriff
news.text:
An alleged trespasser was stopped by private security at a Malibu property belonging to former Vice President Kamala Harris on Friday night, according to local authorities and a Harris spokesperson.

Harris and her husband, Doug Emhoff, were not home at the time, and the person was stopped before reaching the home, according to the spokesperson.

"They are grateful to the security and law enforcement personnel who responded swiftly," the spokesperson said. 

The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department said deputies were called to the property at about 10:30 p.m. local time Friday for a report of a suspicious person. 

"When deputies arrived they made contact with the private security detail on the property," the department said in a statement. "The individual who was outside of the property upon our arrival was warned and advised by deputies to leave the premises and left voluntarily without incident."

No arrest was made. 

The sheriff's office said a trespassing report was taken, and deputies will increase patrols in the area as a precaution.
news.summary: Neither Harris nor her husband, Doug Emhoff, were at the home, according to a spokesperson.

A senior White House official who confirmed the news last August noted that vice presidents typically only get six months of protection after leaving office. That timeline is accurate, as Congress passed a bill in 2008 that cleared Secret Service details for former vice presidents, their spouses and their children under age 16 for up to six months, beginning after the vice president left office, though then-President Joe Biden signed a memorandum in January 2025 extending Harris’ protection to 18 months.

news.title: Woman stopped after entering Kamala Harris' Malibu property
news.text:
A woman entered the Malibu, California, property of former Vice President Kamala Harris and husband Doug Emhoff late on Sept. 11, prompting Harris' security personnel to contact the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department, according to multiple reports.

Security personnel stopped the woman before she reached the home, the Los Angeles Times reported. Harris and Emhoff were not at the property at the time.

Los Angeles County sheriff's deputies responded to the property at about 10:30 p.m., according to Lt. Jason Duron, of the Malibu station. The woman agreed to leave voluntarily and was not arrested.

"We are stepping up patrols of the property to be safe," Duron told the Los Angeles Times.

Why Harris' security has been an issue

The incident comes after changes to Harris' security arrangements following her departure from the White House.

Former vice presidents typically receive six months of Secret Service protection after leaving office. Former President Joe Biden extended Harris' protection, but President Donald Trump revoked the extension in August 2025, according to the Los Angeles Times.

Los Angeles and California law enforcement agencies subsequently helped coordinate security for Harris. The Los Angeles Police Department ended its involvement in September 2025 after criticism over the resources being used to protect the former vice president, the Times reported.

The California Highway Patrol continues to assist Harris' security detail, but CHP officers were not at the Malibu property at the time of the Sept. 11 incident.

Harris' Malibu home

Harris and Emhoff purchased the 4,000-square-foot Malibu home in December 2025 for $8.15 million, according to The Independent. The property is in the secluded Point Dume neighborhood.

In a post to X on Sept. 11, Harris said she and Emhoff were commemorating the 25th anniversary of 9/11 with a visit to Pepperdine University's "Waves of Flags" installation. The school's main campus is in Malibu.

A new poll from Focaldata/Financial Times, released over Labor Day weekend, showed Harris leading Democratic contenders for a potential presidential run in 2028. Harris held a very comfortable lead with 29% support from likely Democratic primary voters in the poll conducted from Aug. 28 to Sept. 2.

A spokesperson for Harris reportedly confirmed to TMZ that the former vice president's security "stopped an individual who illegally entered Vice President Harris and Second Gentleman [Doug] Emhoff's property before the individual reached the home." 

The spokesperson said that neither Harris nor Emhoff were at the residence at the time of the incident. 

“They are grateful to the security and law enforcement personnel who responded swiftly," he told TMZ. 

The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department told the outlet that the incident happened around 10:30 pm at the former vice president's home. The LA Times further confirmed that report. 

The woman who trespassed on the property agreed to leave voluntarily. She was not arrested, according to the LA Times and TMZ, citing law enforcement. 

“We are stepping up patrols of the property to be safe,” LASD Lieutenant Jason Duron told the LA Times. 

Harris and Emhoff bought their Malibu home sometime within the last year. The house reportedly costs more than $8 million. 

It's not the first time the former vice president and her husband have had unwanted visitors approach their homes. 

In January 2025, two individuals were detained during curfew hours at Harris's former home in Brentwood following reports of a possible burglary, according to KTLA. The curfew was in effect due to the Palisades and Eaton fires, which were ravaging the city at the time. 

Neither of the individuals was arrested and no evidence was found suggesting they had committed any crimes.
news.summary: Neither former Vice President Kamala Harris or her husband were home at the time of the incident

news.title: Elon Musk Spends $100 Million on Anti-Trans Ads Targeting Dems in Midterm Races
news.text:
Elon Musk’s America PAC has dropped $100 million to support the GOP in critical races that could control the future of the Senate. It includes TV commercials, digital ads, and a social media blitz across platforms Musk owns and platforms he doesn’t. The eleventh-hour push is a brazen attempt to stoke the anti-trans moral panic and turn equal rights for transgender people into a make-or-break campaign issue.

“The PAC’s emphasis on trans issues is striking because that’s been a much less prominent theme in GOP Senate ads so far this election cycle, per AdImpact, which tracks political advertising,” Axios’s Mike Zapler reports. “On its face, the strategy is at odds with what voters say they want candidates to talk about. Concerns about the economy dominate; trans and LGBT issues barely register. But Republicans remember how lethal the Trump campaign’s ‘Kamala is for they/them ads were to Kamala Harris’ campaign in 2024.”

The ads are a smattering of anti-trans hysterics and culture war talking points attacking James Talarico in Texas, Sherrod Brown in Ohio, Josh Turek in Iowa, Mary Peltola in Alaska, and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. (Musk is also funding some ads in New Hampshire and Maine, but they did not seem to target trans people.) Ads are running on the airwaves, as well as online on sites like Google, Instagram, and Facebook.

With grainy, high-contrast images and ominous music, the ads warn: “James Talarico believes there are six genders.” They said Brown put “the trans agenda ahead of Ohio’s values” and supports “men in women’s sports.” They said Turek “voted to spend our tax dollars on sex change surgeries for children,” that Peltola wants “your daughter to share a bathroom with a man,” and El-Sayed peddles “sex changes for minors.”

This comes after many of these candidates capitulated anyway. Brown put out an ad in 2024 relying on anti-trans stereotypes and grainy images of swimmer Lia Thomas in an apparent attempt to quell right-wing attacks. And Turek recently issued his official statement opposing equal rights for transgender women in sports and his campaign said he further opposed “taxpayer-funded sex changes.” Not to mention early and eager defectors like Rep. Seth Moulton, who left his Massachusetts congressional seat for a failed Senate run, only to be subdued by incumbent Sen. Ed Markey. Polls showed voters in that race were significantly less likely to vote for a candidate who espoused anti-trans and exclusionary views.

None of that stopped Republicans from using the existence of trans people as a cudgel to attack the Democrats and move the conversation further to the right — a strategy explicitly outlined by conservative operatives in the past. Famously, Terry Schilling of the far-right American Principles Project boasted to CNN: “The women’s sports issue was really the beginning point in helping expose all this because what it did was, it got opponents of the LGBT movement comfortable with talking about transgender issues.”

Plans for some sort of major push from the America PAC were first reported in July and August by Axios and The New York Times, respectively. In addition to TV and digital ads, Musk is also expected to aggressively utilize mailer campaigns and door-knocking initiatives to get out the vote in favor of the GOP.

Musk has been a primary antagonist for the trans community for years now. His daughter, model Vivian Wilson, came out as transgender in 2020, infuriating Musk. He once said she “was killed by the woke mind virus” of gender.

“Now, the woke mind virus will die,” Musk continued.

Still, some Democrats are pushing back on Musk’s attempts to bend the election to his own whim. The most prominent example of this might be Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive with a background in health care, whose candidacy has drawn substantial comparisons to that of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Last month, he sparred with Jesse Watters on Fox News, who tried to goad him into a fight about transgender rights. El-Sayed wouldn’t take the bait.

“It’s no surprise that the world’s first trillionaire would be trying to buy a Senate seat,” El-Sayed spokesman Cole Wozniak said in a statement to the local press after Musk’s latest round of ads.

Rather than pivoting on civil rights issues, El-Sayed’s campaign strategy has been to remain laser-focused on the issues that matter most to voters.

“Michiganders will see right through this,” Wozniak said, “and will send Abdul to the Senate this November to take on the corruption by getting money out of politics, putting money in your pocket, and passing Medicare for All.”

This piece was republished with permission from Erin In The Morning.
news.summary: Some of the candidates being targeted have already capitulated to the right on trans rights.
news.author: S. Baum

news.title: Republicans Rally Behind Paxton in Texas With Millions in New Spending
news.text: With less than two months ahead of Election Day, Republican groups are pouring tens of millions of dollars into Texas to bolster state Attorney General Ken Paxton's U.S. Senate bid. A Republican-aligned group known as Texas PAC, which is affiliated with the Senate Leadership Fund, has purchased more than $51 million in advertising supporting Paxton, according to media-tracking firm AdImpact. The spending surge comes as the Texas Senate race has emerged as one of the nation's most closely watched contests, with Democratic candidate James Talarico polling competitively against Paxton. Democrats are eyeing a narrow path to reclaiming control of Congress' upper chamber, where Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority, and are hoping to put the traditionally Republican state in play. To take back the majority, Democrats must defend their current seats—including in two states President Donald Trump won in his 2024 White House bid—and flip four others. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party historically loses seats. Newsweek has reached out to Paxton and Talarico for comment via email on Saturday. Texas Senate Race Texas has backed Republican presidential nominees in every election since 1980, but Democrats hope 2026 will offer one of their best opportunities in years to compete statewide. Trump carried Texas by 13.7 percentage points in 2024, defeating then-Vice President Kamala Harris 56 percent to around 42.5 percent. Texas has not elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994, making it one of the nation's longest-running Republican strongholds. Democrats have repeatedly targeted the state as demographic shifts and population growth have reshaped its electorate, but they have fallen short in a series of closely watched campaigns, including Beto O'Rourke's 2018 Senate bid against Ted Cruz. Polls show Paxton, who is endorsed by Trump, and Talarico, who has served as a state representative since 2018, holding narrow leads at different points in the campaign. The matchup follows Paxton's defeat of longtime Senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary in late May. Republicans descended on Dallas this week for the party’s unprecedented midterm convention. The convention is part of a plan to mobilize the GOP base ahead of November to avert losses in key races, as polls show many Americans have soured on the Trump administration amid growing frustration with inflation, the economy and the Iran war. Spending in the Texas Senate Race The race has become increasingly expensive as national Republicans move to shore up support for Paxton in the campaign's final weeks. Texas PAC has reserved roughly $51.3 million in broadcast television advertising in the Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston, San Antonio and Austin media markets, according to the Texas Tribune, citing AdImpact. Other Republican-aligned groups have also entered the race. MAGA Inc., a Trump-aligned PAC, has reserved about $10 million in Texas advertising, while America PAC, which is backed by Elon Musk, has spent more than $2.6 million on advertising supporting Paxton and opposing Talarico, according to the Tribune. Since the Republican primary, GOP-aligned groups have reserved more than $81 million in advertising backing Paxton, according to AdImpact. Democratic groups and campaigns have reserved about $43.7 million, with much of that spending coming from Talarico's campaign. The Senate Leadership Fund did not include Texas among its targeted Senate races when it unveiled its spending plans in April, noting a marked shift in strategy. Alex Latcham, the head of the Senate Leadership Fund, told The New York Times on Friday that its ad buy “affirms our commitment to maintaining the Republican majority.” Newsweek has filled out a contact request form with the Senate Leadership Fund for comment on Saturday. The late surge of Republican spending follows months in which Talarico enjoyed a substantial financial edge. By the end of June, federal campaign finance filings showed Talarico had approximately $21.5 million in cash on hand, while Paxton reported about $1.75 million. Those same filings showed that Talarico had raised over $68.5 million, compared to Paxton’s $9.2 million. What Polls Show in the Texas Senate Race Forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball consider the race to be a toss-up. A YouGov/Univision poll of 1,000 registered voters conducted between August 27-September 4 found Talarico leading by 5 points, 48 percent to 43 percent. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points. An Overton Insights/Texas Public Policy Foundation poll of 1,167 likely voters from August 24-26 found Talarico and Paxton locked in a statistical dead heat. The poll found Talarico leading with 44 percent support to Paxton's 43.4 percent, while 12.6 percent of respondents remained undecided. When leaners were included, the race was effectively tied, with both candidates receiving 50 percent support. Other recent polling, such as an Emerson College Polling/Nexstar Media poll of 1,000 likely Texas voters, also puts the Senate race in near deadlock, with 47 percent backing Paxton and 46 percent supporting Talarico. About 5 percent are undecided and 2 percent back a different candidate. The poll was conducted August 9-11 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. A Fox News poll of 1,006 registered Texas voters found that 51 percent back Talarico and 48 percent Paxton, with 1 percent undecided. The survey was conducted July 23-27 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. Prediction markets reflect the race's razor-thin margins. As of Saturday afternoon, Kalshi showed Paxton and Talarico tied at 50 percent, while Polymarket gave a slight edge to Talarico at 52 percent. Democrats' Chances of Flipping the Senate Democrats argue that voter concerns about the economy, Trump's declining approval ratings and the war with Iran could create openings in several competitive state races. Despite Democratic optimism, Republicans contend that they will maintain their Senate majority and retain control of Congress. Nationally, 34 percent of voters approve of Trump's job performance while 60 percent disapprove as of Friday, leaving him underwater with a net approval rating of -26, according to Civiqs' rolling online tracking poll of registered voters. As of Saturday, the survey had garnered around 129,500 responses since January 20, 2025 when Trump was inaugurated for a second term. Nate Silver’s Silver Bulletin’s averages show Democrats leading in four races for GOP-held Senate seats, putting the party within reach of the four it needs, but with little room for error. Its latest updated averages show Democrats ahead in Alaska, Georgia, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas. Republicans lead in Florida, Iowa and Kansas. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Hollie Silverman and Anthony Murray.
news.summary: A Republican-aligned group known as Texas PAC has purchased more than $51 million in advertising supporting Paxton.
news.author: Mandy Taheri

news.title: Trespasser stopped on former Vice President Kamala Harris' Malibu property
news.text: A trespasser tried to enter former Vice President Kamala Harris' cliffside home in Malibu on Friday evening, according to the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department and a Harris spokesman. Harris and her husband, Doug Emhoff, were not home at the time, according to Eduardo Negrón, a spokesperson for Harris. He did not respond to a question about the couple's whereabouts. "Last night, security personnel stopped an individual who illegally entered Vice President Harris and Second Gentleman Emhoff's property before the individual reached the home," he said in a statement. "They are grateful to the security and law enforcement personnel who responded swiftly." Harris' on-site security contacted the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department, which has jurisdiction over Malibu. Lt. Jason Duron, a watch commander at the Malibu/Lost Hills sheriff's station, said his department was contacted by Harris' security detail when a woman attempted to enter the property. Sheriff's deputies responded around 10:30 p.m., and the woman, who has not been identified, agreed to leave voluntarily. She was not arrested. "We are stepping up patrols of the property to be safe," Duron said. Harris' level of security has previously been scrutinized. Former vice presidents typically receive six months of Secret Service protection after leaving office, but former President Biden extended the coverage. President Trump, who beat Harris in the 2024 election, revoked the extension in August 2025. That led Los Angeles and California law enforcement agencies to scramble to protect Harris. The Los Angeles Police Department quickly discontinued its involvement amid criticism that shifting manpower to protect the former vice president was hampering the agency's ability to fight crime. The California Highway Patrol continues to assist Harris’ security detail, but its officers were not on-site Friday night, according to CHP Sgt. Christian Stevens.
news.summary: A trespasser tried to enter former Vice President Kamala Harris' cliffside property in Malibu.
news.author: Seema Mehta

From Flatley's flute to 'vicious b*stards': The view from inside Trump's big tent 

500 of Ireland’s business leaders, diplomats, political and public figures gathered for an audience with Trump earlier today.

7.47pm, 12 Sep 2026

Share options

Niall O'Connor

reports from Deerfield

DONALD TRUMP NORMALLY finds himself flanked by heavily armed Secret Service officers and bulletproof glass when he takes to the stage. 

But not when he spoke this morning to 500 of Ireland’s business leaders, diplomats, political and public figures.

It was a perfect example of how being inside the tent is always better than out, as rain and wind battered the massive marquee set up in the grounds of the US Ambassador’s residence in the Phoenix Park.

Well-heeled attendees – women in expensive frocks and men in well-tailored suits – mingled as they awaited the US president’s arrival, and it was clear this wasn’t an Irish political party’s local cumann meeting.

In stark contrast to the outside world, the security bubble at Deerfield in the Phoenix Park, home to Ambassador Edward Walsh, was more about keeping the outside world away than looking out for a rogue element inside the tent. 

Trump’s Presidential emblazoned lectern was remarkably close to the gathered mass of VVIPs sitting on seats and the mere VIPs standing at the back.

The VVIP’s were made up of representatives from multi-billion euro companies such as Google and Amazon, Irish food firm Ornua, Intel and other tech giants based in Dublin. Waterford Crystal was represented and former ministers Simon Coveney and Mary Hanafin were spotted in the crowd.

Guests at Deerfield this morning.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

There were also other political figures, led by Micheál Martin and his wife Mary, as well as ex-Taoisigh like Enda Kenny and Bertie Ahern. 

State officials were also present with secretaries general from the departments of transport, defence, energy and transport. 

The Chief of Staff of the Irish Defence Forces Lt Gen Rossa Mulcahy and Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly were also spotted. 

Advertisement

Eddie Hobbs, the well-known Cork financial advice guru, sat next to Niamh Uí Bhrian, a co-owner of the Gript website.

Billionaires Denis O’Brien and Dermot Desmond were also on the guest list for the VVIPs. Ambassadors from Britain, Australia and Canada were seated close to them, while Morocco and Georgian delegates were also present. 

Amidst the VIPs were former and serving TDs and current senators. Former independent TD Cathal Berry was there, as was Senator Gerry Craughwell. Independent Ireland TDs Michael Collins and Ken O’Flynn also made an appearance, as did Fianna Fáil’s James O’Connor. 

The Journal / YouTube

Inside the tent

As the morning wore on, musicians played traditional Irish songs and a mix of folk standards – the kind of songs you might find in a tourist trap pub in Temple Bar.

At one stage VVIP Michael Flatley, who was accompanied by his son Michael St James Flatley, took to the stage and was interviewed by master of ceremonies Alan Shortt about his interest in boxing, his upbringing in Chicago and his Irish parents being migrants. He was keen to stress they entered the US legally in 1947. 

Flatley later produced his flute and entertained the guests with an upbeat tune. (The Lord of the Dance star, before he became internationally known, was an All Ireland Flute Championship winner for three years running in the mid-1970s).

When the musicians were taking a break a Donald Trump playlist of songs from his rallies in the United States was played. 

The songs were as eclectic as the gathered guests – by artists such as Guns and Roses, Elvis, the Backstreet Boys and Pavarotti.

While they waited the guests chatted and made connections inside the tent and outside over coffee.

Business cards were swapped, and phone numbers exchanged. 

President Donald Trump arrives to deliver remarks to U.S. embassy staff at Deerfield Residence in Dublin.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

Trump arrives 

Trump and his cavalcade arrived late by about 45 minutes following an extended visit to Farmleigh.

'Why on Earth would we welcome him?': Thousands take to Dublin streets to protest 'warmonger' Trump

A frenzied and apparently frazzled White House press corps burst in as Trump met and posed for photographs with some of the VVIPs inside the residence. 

Walsh took to the stage to tell the audience he had the “best job” and spoke of his affection for his friend Donald. 

With that he welcomed Trump on the platform. Trump pouted and posed for a bit and then launched into one of his usual, rambling speeches. 

It was a diatribe against his political enemies like Joe Biden and Kamala Harris and included stories of supposed triumphant wars in the Middle East and Venezuela. 

It was for all the world a classic Trump rally speech and at times not lacking in some humour as he poked fun at his own friends and joked about how he never cheats at golf because of his Secret Service protection detail. That got a big laugh, especially when he then said he was not averse to cheating. 

During the more US-focused rantings, some of the VIPs started to show an increased interest in their well-polished shoes, but he appeared to win the room back over with praise for Irish business and investment in the US. 

He finished it off with a comment much like that infamous Páidí Ó Sé’s compliment to Kerry fans as “the roughest type of fucking animals you could ever deal with”.

Trump got laughter as he said Irish people were friendly but “vicious bastards” and then a cheer when he spoke of Shane Lowry and Rory McIllroy. It was said not as an insult but as an appreciation for how he viewed Ireland. 

He declared his need to get to Doonbeg, and off he walked to the tune of the Village People’s YMCA.

The VVIPs and VIPs mingled as they queued for buses to get them back to their cars, as Trump headed for Dublin Airport and his Qatari gifted Air Force One to ferry him to the real focus of the trip – the Irish Open, where’s he’s kept a somewhat lower profile. 

Niall O'Connor

news.title: Shelly Headen and the Ghosts of Internets Past
news.text:
First, let me apologize for yesterday's history segment being out of sequence. My bad, I grabbed the wrong file. NOW, it's correct. (Sigh)

There are jobs in this country that tend to go unfilled. So desperate are employers to fill those roles that "They have a pulse" is the sole qualifier.

I've long since started to wonder if the Democrat Party isn't just that desperate. Every election cycle produces at least one, and usually far more candidates who make you wonder whether the opposition party secretly recruited them as a plant. With that in mind, allow me to introduce you to Shelly Headen.

She's an accountant from Oak Ridge, N.C., and the Democrat nominee challenging Republican state Rep. John Blust (R-N.C.) in Guilford County's House District 62 — one of the races Republicans are watching closely as they try to hold their majority. The official candidate list confirms Headen and Blust as the two names on the ballot.

And then came the social-media archaeology, because apparently nobody in modern politics has bothered explaining to candidates that the internet remembers everything, forever, whether you'd like it to or not.

Resurfaced posts bearing Headen's name and photo included comparisons of Donald Trump to Hitler, rhetoric flirting with political violence, and assorted other charmers. Standard Democrat talking points, in other words, just with the volume turned all the way up. But the crown jewel arrived Friday, when Breitbart reported on a Facebook post from a European vacation. PJM's Catherine Salgado reported on it here on Friday.

Headen had visited the Dachau concentration camp memorial. In the photo, she's smiling in front of the crematorium ovens. Her caption: "Visiting Dauchau [sic] Concentration Camp in Germany… This is where Trump supporters belong."

Honey, that's spelled Dachau, for starters. Second, and rather more urgently: that's the site where the Nazis imprisoned, tortured, and murdered human beings by the thousands. Headen's caption apparently proposed the same treatment for her political opponents. Was it meant as a joke? Doesn't much matter — the comment lands equally badly regardless of intent, standing in front of those ovens.

Mind you, this wasn't some isolated brain cramp floating around in the ether. According to The Assembly, Headen had also written, after Kamala Harris accepted the 2024 nomination, "I'm so excited! Ready for the MAGAs to die off!!" The Assembly further reported Headen acknowledged being "very vocal against MAGA," while insisting that she couldn't recall the specific language she'd used. Bold defense strategy. "I don't remember saying that" rarely lands well when the evidence in question is sitting online wearing your own name tag.

But wait, there's more, because there always is. Headen said she'd paid a consulting firm $30,000 to comb her own social-media history for potential landmines. Thirty thousand dollars, spent specifically to catch exactly this kind of disaster before it detonated — and the consultants somehow strolled right past their client posing gleefully in front of the ovens at Dachau. If that's what passes for due diligence, one has to wonder what actually made the cut, and shudder a little imagining how she'd handle an actual budget with real taxpayer money attached to it.

Then there's the other little problem. Headen reportedly denied ever having an X account, despite the North Carolina House Democratic Caucus itself having linked to an account bearing her name earlier this year. At that point, this stopped being "candidate says something dumb on Facebook" and graduated to a full-blown political fire drill.

Even WFDD, the NPR affiliate, picked up the story. The North Carolina House Democratic Caucus subsequently withdrew its support outright, its spokesman calling Headen's posts "unacceptable" and out of step with the party's expectations for its candidates. The Guilford County Democrat Party piled on next, yanking its financial, operational, and organizational support, and calling the comments "completely indefensible." Republican House Speaker Destin Hall summed it up about as efficiently as anyone: "absolutely disgusting."

Which raises the obvious question: exactly how badly does a Democrat candidate have to embarrass himself or herself before his or her own party would rather hand the seat to a Republican? Apparently, this badly.

But hold on. There's still more, and the "more" might be the single most extraordinary part of the whole saga: Headen's stated reason for staying in the race invokes Jesus Christ, Martin Luther King Jr., and Abraham Lincoln, all in one breath. "I've sacrificed myself just like Jesus sacrificed himself on the cross, and Martin Luther King and Abraham Lincoln and all the people that put themselves out there to sacrifice for our country," she said. "If a few angry moments on social media are the end, then so be it."

There are moments in politics where you genuinely can't tell whether you're watching a campaign unfold or an audition for a Monty Python sketch. Comparing a string of ill-advised social-media posts to the crucifixion, the civil rights movement, and a presidential assassination is one way to establish perspective. "Unconventional" would be the generous word for it. Longtime readers will know I don't tend to be quite so generous.

Here's the practical wrinkle that keeps this from simply fading away: Headen remains on the ballot. North Carolina law places hard deadlines on candidate withdrawal, and the State Board of Elections confirms that a nominee can't simply resign from a general-election ballot outside the statutory process once nominated. State candidate records still list Headen and Blust as the two names in District 62.

So even with the entire party apparatus backing away in horror, Headen remains the official Democrat nominee — producing the genuinely delightful spectacle of a party effectively whispering, "Please, don't vote for our own candidate," while her name sits printed right next to the party label on every ballot in the district. You couldn't invent this if you tried, and if you did, an editor would send it back for being too bizarre.

That's exactly why the Shelly Headen story earns more than a passing chuckle. Yes, she's one candidate in one North Carolina House district. But she's far from the only candidate this cycle whose baggage has become a headache for the people who nominated her.

Look at Maine, where Graham Platner's Senate campaign piled up controversy after controversy — inflammatory posts, a tattoo resembling a Nazi symbol, allegations over his treatment of women, and eventually a rape allegation he denied. Democratic support collapsed by degrees until Platner suspended his campaign outright.

Or look at Michigan, where Democrat Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed faces his own entirely separate pile of controversy — past statements, political associations, and his relationship with a certain controversial streaming provocateur we've already spent considerable column space on. His campaign is now under sustained Republican fire over exactly those associations.

Then there's James Talarico (D-Tex., Senate) — video resurfaced of him rejecting "tough on crime" policies in 2020, followed by more video of him thanking activists for drawing a "link between climate change and white supremacy and capitalism." Separately, a resurfaced 2022 speech showed him announcing his campaign would purchase only vegan products — instant backlash in a state that treats barbecue as a civic religion. Ted Cruz piled on directly: "This freak wants to ban BBQ." Talarico's team responded by posting a photo of him eating a turkey leg, and he later got laughs on a live podcast declaring, "I deny all accusations of veganism."

There’s Mallory McMorrow (D-Mich., Senate) — CNN unearthed decade-old deleted tweets showing views well to the left of her current moderate positioning, including complaining "I don't like you, Michigan" about the state's weather shortly after moving there from California, and declaring "cars are dead" — a genuinely rough line to have on record while courting voters in the heart of the American auto industry. Her defense: the old posts prove she's a "regular person" who wasn't carefully curating a political image years before running.

There also Will Lawrence (D-Mich., 7th District primary) — deleted 2020 tweets backing "defund the police" resurfaced, including a 2021 follow-up post reading: "Seems like cops are bad at stopping crime, hey i've got an idea, let's get rid of them and try something else." He's since tried distancing himself, insisting voters would see through what he calls "stupid political games" once they get to know him.

Add Darializa Avila Chevalier to this mess. Semafor groups her alongside Lawrence and Platner as another progressive candidate this cycle who deleted controversial posts that later resurfaced anyway.

These share a genuinely modern political problem: Candidates are carrying years of digital history into races that didn't exist when they wrote any of it. Twitter, Facebook, Instagram, podcasts, Reddit, YouTube, old text messages, deleted posts, five-year-old photographs — all of it is potential ammunition, and the people running these campaigns absolutely know it.

Which makes the Headen episode particularly hard to explain away. She reportedly spent $30,000 having someone dig through her own digital past looking for precisely this kind of landmine. And the political equivalent of a corpse turned up in the closet anyway — a genuinely enormous corpse, wearing a name tag, standing in front of the ovens at Dachau, smiling for the camera. This raises two serious questions, both about how carefully and effectively she will spend tax dollars, and of course her underlying political and moral philosophies… you know, the ones she tried at great expense to hide.

Look, I'm not without fault. My admission at the top of this page proves that much at least. But how many times does this need to happen, in exactly the same direction, before we can label it a trend? And to the Democrat Party, I offer this advice: It's called "Vetting your candidates." You might wanna look into it. Particularly if you're trying to hide the truth from the voters.
