news.title: Who Is the Democratic Party's Headliner?
news.text:
Hello, and welcome to Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026. 

My calendar says it's the Day of Encouragement, Video Games Day, Chocolate Milkshake Day, Hug and High Five Day, and Iguana Awareness Day. Encourage somebody, blend up a chocolate milkshake, hug a friend and high-five a stranger, and give an iguana its due respect — busy little Saturday.

Today in history: 1609:English explorer Henry Hudson sails up the river that now bears his name.1846: Elizabeth Barrett secretly marries Robert Browning at St. Marylebone Church in London.1914: The First Battle of the Marne ends in an Allied victory against Germany, halting the initial German advance in World War I.1938: Adolf Hitler demands self-determination for the Sudeten Germans in Czechoslovakia, escalating tensions that lead to war within the year.1942: A German U-boat torpedoes the RMS Laconia off West Africa, killing more than 1,600 people before an American bomber attacks the German rescue effort, prompting Germany to ban future rescues of survivors at sea.1943: German paratroopers free Benito Mussolini from the hotel where the Italian government is holding him.1953: Massachusetts Sen. John F. Kennedy marries Jacqueline Bouvier in Newport, Rhode Island.1960: Democratic presidential candidate John F. Kennedy addresses concerns about his Catholic faith before a Houston ministers' group, telling them, "I do not speak for my church on public matters, and the church does not speak for me."1974: Ethiopia's military deposes Emperor Haile Selassie after 58 years of rule.1977: South African student leader Steven Biko dies in police custody, triggering an international outcry.1992: The space shuttle Endeavour launches, carrying the first married couple in space and Mae Jemison, the first black woman in space.

Birthdays Today include: H.L. Mencken, writer, journalist, critic; Yao Ming, NBA Hall of Famer; Barry White, singer ("You're the First, the Last, My Everything"); Emmy Rossum, actor (Shameless).

If today's your birthday too, happy birthday — you're in good company.

Here's a question that has more weight than you might think: If Democrats were to hold a midterm convention along the lines of the one Republicans just held, who would be the headliner? More to the point: Who could they put on that stage who actually embodies where the Democrat Party is going? Not merely who polls well. Not merely who holds an important office. Not merely who can deliver a reasonably competent speech. Who is the person around whom the movement itself is coalescing?

The question sounds academic until you think about what a political convention is actually supposed to accomplish. It isn't simply a four-day infomercial. At its best, a convention tells voters: “This is who we are. This is where we're going. And this is the person who best represents it.”

Republicans have an obvious answer: Donald Trump's MAGA. That doesn't mean every Republican agrees with everything Trump says or does. It doesn't mean every Republican candidate wants to make every race a referendum on Trump. But there is no serious question about who the center of gravity of today's Republican Party is. The GOP can put Trump on a stage, and everybody in the room knows why he's there.

And yes, Trump is done in two years. But even Democrats seem to feel the GOP bench is far deeper. We're not going to have much trouble coming up with a MAGA Republican to run for POTUS, or any of the congressional seats. 

Now ask the same question of Democrats. Who gets the microphone?

Gavin Newsom? I doubt it.

Newsom certainly has national visibility, and he has been cultivating a national profile with increasingly aggressive attacks on Trump. His political operation is plainly looking beyond Sacramento. But there's a problem: the disaster that is California. The same state that provides Newsom his platform also hands his opponents an enormous amount of ammunition. And while Newsom can generate attention, attention isn't the same thing as movement leadership. His national profile still depends heavily on the very thing Democrats supposedly want to move past: Donald Trump. Beyond his opposition to Trump, he isn't bringing much else to the table. That's a weak foundation on which to build a post-Trump political identity.

Kamala Harris? Uhhhhhh…. no.

Giggles is probably the least likely to be what I will call a movement leader, or a “spiritual leader.” She's currently the nominal frontrunner by the numbers — leading most 2028 primary polls, usually in the high-20s to low-40s, depending on the pollster, and running strongest with black voters, the most important bloc in a Democrat primary. But leading the polls and leading a movement are two different things, which is precisely the distinction this entire discussion turns on. Harris represents the most recent defeat. That, among Democrats, is the kiss of death. Putting her on a midterm convention stage would read less as "this is who we are becoming" and more as "we're re-litigating the loss of 2024" — which is close to the last thing vulnerable House Democrats running in swing districts would want as their backdrop. In truth, the only thing she’s got going on for her is that she is the anti-Kelly candidate for the role. And I’ll get to Kelly. In the end, Harris might be the most plausible nominee, but she doesn’t answer the question of what comes after Trump, policy-wise. She ran on that question in 2024 and lost not only the White House, but both houses of Congress as well. And by the way, that she's the most plausible candidate doesn't speak well for the rest of the Democrat stable, now, does it?

Hakeem Jeffries? Again, I don't see it.

Jeffries holds House Democrat leadership, and that makes him important. But institutional importance and movement leadership are two different things. He has to balance a caucus containing both progressives and centrists while presenting a unified national message. That's a difficult job. It doesn't exactly scream movement.

Ken Martin? (Dry chuckle) Not a chance.

Martin is a party mechanic, and that's not an insult — parties need mechanics. They need people who understand organization, fundraising, state parties, candidate recruitment and the thousand small pieces that have to fit together to make a national political operation function. But nobody shows up at a rally because Ken Martin is speaking. He's the guy who runs the building, not the guy who fills it. He's furniture, not a focal point, and furniture rarely starts political movements. Besides, most Dems are still ticked at his handling of 2024, and the resulting autopsy report. Hard no.

Mark Kelly? No. More interesting, but he also comes out a hard no.

Kelly has a biography that practically writes its own campaign ad: astronaut, combat pilot, senator, husband of Gabby Giffords, a figure with genuine personal credibility on guns and violence. His 2024 convention remarks leaned heavily on his military and space background, and the idea of teamwork and national strength. But there's a difference between an impressive biography and political magnetism. Kelly's political identity is built largely around competence, moderation and pragmatism. And of course, let's not forget his well-entrenched case of Trump Derangement Syndrome. That's a recognizable political lane. But a movement requires something else: emotional identification. It requires people to look at the person on the stage and say, That's us. Kelly doesn't have that.

And that brings us to Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

AOC unquestionably has something the others lack: base energy. She generates enthusiasm, at least among the hard left. Certainly, she’s strongly identified as a victim of Trump Derangement Syndrome. She has a recognizable political identity and a substantial following among the activist wing of the Democratic coalition, and she can produce the sort of emotional response that makes politics feel like something more than a committee meeting. But that's also the problem. The Democratic institutional establishment — and particularly its donors — have never fully embraced her as the party's national face. And that tells us something: The people paying the bills view her as a nice face with little else behind it. In short, the proverbial DEI hire.

Democrats have plenty of politicians. They have plenty of people who can raise money, generate headlines, give a speech, poll reasonably well. But do they have someone who can stand in front of the entire coalition and say, This is where we're going? That's the question, and it's a very different one from "Who is leading the polls?" The distinction matters.

The leader of a political movement isn't necessarily whoever currently holds the highest office or has the highest name recognition. Sometimes the person who defines a party's future appears before the party itself is ready to recognize it.

Consider Ronald Reagan's challenge to Gerald Ford in 1976 as one example of how a movement can exist inside a party before it controls the party. Reagan lost the nomination, but the ideological conflict exposed a changing Republican coalition — a split significant enough, I'd argue, to help hand the country the disaster that was Jimmy Carter. Four years later, Reagan was the Republican nominee and won by overwhelming numbers. Establishment GOP types and the Democrats both have never gotten over that.

Barack Obama offers a cleaner example. His keynote at the 2004 Democratic National Convention didn't make him the nominee. But it introduced a national audience to a politician who would become the party's standard-bearer just four years later. That's what I mean by a spiritual leader.

And by "spiritual," I don't mean religious. I mean the person who gives a political coalition its sense of identity — who doesn't merely tell the party what it believes, but makes its supporters believe he understands what they believe.

That is something Donald Trump possesses in abundance. Whatever else one thinks of Trump, there is no ambiguity about his relationship to the contemporary Republican movement. The GOP's 2026 midterm convention made that explicit, with Trump placing himself at the center of the party's congressional campaign message.

Democrats don't appear to have an equivalent figure. And that raises a far more important question than who would give the keynote address: Are Democrats actually leaderless? I'm not suggesting Democrats lack leaders. They obviously don't. What they may lack is a movement focal point. Those are not the same thing.

One could argue that 2018 provides Democrats a counterargument — that they don't necessarily need a single charismatic figure to win a midterm election. The Democratic resistance to Trump that year was diffuse. It wasn't organized around one national tribune. It was an anti-Trump movement involving activists, candidates, women's groups, suburban voters, progressive organizations and a wide assortment of local and national figures. Brookings' contemporary analysis described the period as one of unusually intense Democratic mobilization, with large numbers of candidates entering races and organizations expanding their efforts.

And it worked.

From that, you might conclude Democrats don't need a Trump — that "anti-Trump" is enough. There's a problem with that theory, though: They already tried it.

In 2024, opposition to Trump was again central to the Democratic message. Once again, the was no focal point beyond Trump hate. The Democratic convention itself explicitly framed the choice around Trump versus the Harris-Walz vision for the country. And Democrats lost. Which brings us to the more fundamental problem.

What comes after "No Trump"? That's the question Democrats still haven't answered convincingly from 2024. I suggest it’s mostly because they don’t have that answer. They can tell us what they oppose. They can tell us what they fear. They can tell us what they think Trump represents and what they believe Republicans are doing wrong. But what is the affirmative vision? Where is the destination? And, perhaps most important, who represents it?

One faction of the Democratic coalition has a very clear answer, and that faction spells real trouble in a general election: the Democratic Socialists of America and the broader socialist left have a vision. They want the Democrat Party — or at least a significant portion of it — to move substantially further left on economics, government and social policy. That's a non-starter for the average American voter, and with the votes in the last few cycles running close to 50/50, particularly for the all-important swing voter. 

The people who represent the institutional center don't necessarily inspire the activist base. And the people who might appeal to swing voters don't necessarily generate much ideological enthusiasm. The result is a split Democrat Party, and a loss come 2028.

If you put the people listed above on a stage and ask, "Which one of you represents the future of the Democratic movement?," I'm convinced there's no clear answer among Democrats. And if there isn't, that's not merely a problem with the convention program. That's a problem with the party itself.

The key element here is that voters, particularly swing voters, notice these things, and elections are won and lost on those points.

Thought of the Day: To trust someone with your future, you need to know where they're going to take you.

news.title: Democrats are within striking distance in the Senate, but shouldn't celebrate yet
news.text: If the 2026 midterms were held today, polls suggest that Democrats would be the favorites to retake the Senate. Indeed, according to RealClearPolitics polling averages, Democratic Senate candidates lead in North Carolina (+8%), Minnesota (+4%), Texas (+3%), Ohio (+3%), as well as Michigan, Maine, and Alaska (+2% each). Moreover, with President Trump’s approval rating hovering just below 40%, it’s legitimate to ask whether his sagging approval numbers will drag down Republican candidates across the country. 12 RACES SCRAMBLE SENATE BATTLEFIELD AS DEMOCRATS EYE COMEBACK Needing to flip four seats — assuming no GOP pickups in Michigan, Minnesota, or Georgia — the Senate is well within striking distance for Democrats, according to the data. That being said, the midterms are not today, and roughly two months until Election Day is a considerable amount of time. In that same vein, the Democratic candidates in these races have a number of personal and party-wide vulnerabilities, so it is by no means clear that what may currently look possible — or even probable — will come to fruition. TRUMP'S APPROVAL RATING PLUMMETS TO NEW LOW AHEAD OF CRITICAL MIDTERMS: 'MORE WORK TO DO' I say this for a number of reasons. First, outside of North Carolina and Texas, in each state, the Democrats’ polling advantages are well within the margin of error. Voters tend to turn their attention to midterms only after the summer ends, so it is entirely conceivable that these numbers reflect high-frequency voters, which often benefits Democrats. Second, and perhaps more important, frustration with the Trump administration will only get Democrats so far — candidate quality remains a deciding factor for many moderates and swing voters. LEE CARTER: THE SUMMER POLLS MISSED THE POINT: VOTERS ARE MOVING — AND THE MIDTERMS BEGIN The success of candidates affiliated with, or members of, the Democratic Socialists of America has opened a lane for Republicans to paint all Democrats as out-of-touch, far-left extremists. In 2024, then-candidate Donald Trump effectively painted former Vice President Kamala Harris as too far left on hot-button social issues, and Democrats have only moved further left since. DEMOCRATIC INFIGHTING GROWS AS CONGRESSWOMAN EXPOSES ‘DISRESPECTFUL’ WELCOME OF SOCIALISTS INTO ‘BIG TENT’ On this, races in Texas, Michigan, and Maine in particular will be crucial to watch and may represent Republicans’ best hope of maintaining control of the upper chamber. As I’ve noted previously in these pages, the Democrats in those races — James Talarico, Abdul El-Sayed, and Troy Jackson, respectively — are so far to the political left that it’s easy to see how voters could be turned off. SENATE MAP TIGHTENS AS TOP FORECASTER MOVES 3 RACES TOWARD DEMOCRATS Whether it’s Talarico’s past support for transgender women competing against biological girls in sports, El-Sayed’s anti-American statements, his rabid anti-Israel positions, his association with far-left Twitch influencer Hasan Piker, or Jackson’s history of flip-flopping and other controversies, these are flawed candidates. To that end, as these campaigns kick off in earnest, Republicans are all but certain to remind voters of their opponents’ far-left progressive positions on a number of issues. GOP SENATOR, EX-HOUSE DEM EMERGE FROM ALASKA’S ‘JUNGLE PRIMARY’ DESPITE FAR-LEFT MEDDLING Even when the Democrat is not a progressive, such as in Alaska, where Mary Peltola is a moderate Blue Dog Democrat, Republicans may be able to tie all Democrats to the DSA. That’s been Republican Dan Sullivan’s strategy, framing a vote for Peltola as a vote for a Senate hostile to the state’s energy sector — a vital local issue — despite Peltola’s record of supporting drilling. Third, on a basic level, Democrats’ task is made more difficult by needing to secure 51 seats given Vice President JD Vance’s tiebreaking vote and the possibility that Sen. John Fetterman could switch parties. He has repeatedly denied any intention of doing so, though his video appearance at the GOP convention in Dallas on Wednesday did nothing to quell rumors or speculation. Finally, Republicans have a sizable cash advantage. In recent filings, the Republican National Committee reported $128.5 million in cash on hand, versus $16.3 million for the DNC. FORMER DSA MEMBER ALLEGES COMMUNISTS HAVE ‘CAPTURED’ SOCIALIST GROUP, WARNS DEMOCRATIC PARTY IS NEXT Additionally, across the three major Republican committees and two affiliated super PACs, Republicans reported $657 million — nearly double the $334 million held by comparable Democratic groups. President Trump’s super PAC alone has more than $400 million. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Ultimately, Democrats have a genuine chance to retake the Senate, a remarkable achievement just two years after their 2024 across-the-board defeat. The 2026 Senate map had been considered favorable to Republicans, but, according to the polls, it’s Democrats who have the momentum. That Democratic candidates would be leading in Senate races in states like Alaska and Texas would have been inconceivable not long ago. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP However, the midterms are by no means a foregone conclusion, and a polling lead two months before Election Day is not the same as winning the election. Democrats’ razor-thin margins in the majority of the states they need, lingering concerns over candidate quality and the DSA’s impact, as well as Republicans’ massive financial advantage, mean it is by no means clear that the Senate will flip. Carly Cooperman is CEO of Schoen Cooperman Research. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM DOUG SCHOEN
news.summary: Democrats are within striking distance of flipping the Senate, but razor-thin margins and candidate flaws in Texas, Michigan, and Maine loom large.

news.title: Trump ally in Wisconsin sticks close to the president as Democrats push to flip swing district
news.text:
READSTOWN, Wis. (AP) — The way Derrick Van Orden sees it, any Republicans in the U.S. House who distance themselves from President Donald Trump in this year's midterm election aren't just being foolish, they're being disloyal.

That’s why Van Orden, a two-term incumbent from western Wisconsin fighting to keep his seat in November in a swing district Trump carried three times, is embracing the president. 

It’s a risky gambit given fears among Republicans that Trump’s sagging polling numbers, the unpopular Iran war and economic concerns will drag them down. But it reflects a calculation by Van Orden, a former Navy SEAL who embodies the president's confrontational politics, that motivating the conservative base is still the best plan as long as Trump remains the party’s undisputed leader.

“There’s something that’s sorely lacking in this political business and it’s loyalty," Van Orden told The Associated Press before flying to Dallas to appear at Trump's midterm convention this week. "I think we’d be a lot better off if we were more loyal to our fellow Americans to begin with.”

Van Orden faces Democrat Rebecca Cooke, a political activist who grew up on a dairy farm and works part time as a restaurant server. It’s a rematch of a race that Van Orden won by less than 3 percentage points two years ago.

Wisconsin’s 3rd Congressional District is one of a dwindling number of competitive U.S. House races that could be pivotal to Democrats' hopes of recapturing control of Congress.

The race is in ‘a bellwether district in a bellwether state’

The V-shaped district is bordered by the Mississippi River and Minnesota to the west and Illinois to the south. It historically has been supportive of moderates such as Democrat Ron Kind, who held the seat for 26 years before retiring in 2022. Before him, a moderate Republican represented the district for 16 years.

Democrat Barack Obama won the district twice in his White House races. Trump won it three times on his way to narrowly carrying Wisconsin in 2016 and 2024 and losing the state in 2020.

U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who has had his share of slim victories over the years, has called it “a bellwether district in a bellwether state.”

Cooke and Van Orden have been crisscrossing the district and they both ended up at the same place for a Labor Day parade, in the tiny village of Readstown. It's in the rolling hills of the Driftless Area and is home to fewer than 500 people.

Cooke told the AP before walking in the parade that she believes voters this year are “looking for something fresh and something different. I think people are very tired of politics as usual.”

Nancy Deckert, a 75-year-old retired post office worker in Readstown, is just the type of voter Cooke is counting on.

“I think a lot of people are fed up with the mess we’re in right now and a change is what we need,” Deckert said at the parade.

Van Orden rode his 2021 Harley-Davidson motorcycle along the parade route before parking outside the Shovelheads Corner Bar.

The bar's owner, John Collett, said he is voting for Van Orden.

“It’s popular to hate America right now, and that’s unfortunate,” said Collett, who called himself “ultra MAGA,” a reference to Trump's “Make America Great Again” movement. Collett said Van Orden is “fighting for the American people. He’s fighting for what’s right.”

Van Orden, who underperformed Trump in 2024, said he is confident that voters like Collett will stick with him.

“Cooke knows that she needs to have people who voted for Trump vote for her,” Van Orden said, “and that just ain’t happening.”

Van Orden is embracing Trump while other Republicans seek distance

Van Orden voted with Trump nearly 100% of the time in 2025, and Trump named Van Orden as one of several House Republicans he promised to back “100% all the way to November.” America PAC, connected to tech titan Elon Musk, has spent about $10,000 this month for Van Orden, Federal Election Commission documents show.

Trump's only visit to Wisconsin so far in his second term was to Van Orden's district. Top administration members have come to campaign with Van Orden, including Trump's health secretary, Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., FBI Director Kash Patel and Dr. Mehmet Oz, who leads the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.

Cooke said it was a “big mistake” for Van Orden to tie himself so closely to Trump in a state where only about 4 in 10 voters approve of Trump’s performance, based on an August poll conducted by the Marquette University Law School. 

Van Orden said he does not have any second thoughts about it. 

“I’ve done everything I possibly can to help the people here in the 3rd (District) and to help Wisconsinites and help Americans,” Van Orden said. “And if people in the 3rd Congressional District decide they want to have somebody else who is a rampant socialist to represent them, that’s up to them.”

Van Orden spoke on Wednesday at the Republican convention, which was billed as “Trump-a-Palooza.” Van Orden promoted tax cuts and federal spending on rural healthcare, a big issue in a district where the largest city is only about 72,000 people. 

The congressman attended the Jan. 6, 2021, rally before a mob of Trump supporters stormed the U.S. Capitol. He has had a series of high-profile incidents and is known for exchanging sometimes profanity-laden messages with liberal U.S. Rep. Mark Pocan, D-Wis., and others over social media. This year, Van Orden has drawn heat for a series of artificial intelligence-generated videos that show faked images of Cooke saying things she did not actually say. Van Orden has defended them as satire. 

“I’m super easy to demonize because I am very aggressive on social media,” Van Orden said. But he said he does it because of death threats made against him and his family.

“When you push back on these folks they stop and when you let them go they get emboldened,” he said. “I’m not getting pushed around by anybody.”

Cooke is looking to build a broad coalition of Democrats and independents

Cooke lost to Van Orden by just over 11,000 votes two years ago while performing better than Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris and Democratic U.S. Sen. Tammy Baldwin. 

The environment is “really different” this year, Cooke said, and that will put her over the top.

“People are really frustrated and disappointed with the Trump administration and the things that they were promised," she said.

Cooke, who formerly owned a small business and ran a nonprofit aimed at helping women-owned businesses, is trying to pitch herself as a big tent Democratic populist. But Van Orden points to her work as a consultant raising money for Democrats across the country as far back as 2012, saying she will be beholden to the party establishment. 

She is endorsed by a broad coalition including the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, more moderate groups like the House Blue Dog PAC and progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. He campaigned with Cooke in the district last year, giving her the blessing of the party's progressive wing while also helping to fend off Van Orden's attack that she's the “anointed” candidate of the Democratic Washington establishment.

Van Orden, in a campaign ad, is also going after Cooke for saying if she lived in New York City she would have supported democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani for mayor. In that same ad, Van Orden holds a firearm, displays a Bible and says, “I fought extremists overseas as a Navy SEAL, but now they are here.”

Dean Young, a 75-year-old former teacher and milk truck driver who lives in a rural area near Readstown, called the ad “unbelievable."

“People are getting angry,” Young said from a lawn chair along the parade route, a dog in his lap. “They’re finally starting to suffer. I think that’s going to lead to some change.”

news.title: What Trump has wrought on a Dallas convention floor
news.text:
DALLAS — Donald Trump’s hold on the Republican Party is near total, and for two days this week, it filled an arena. A decade in politics has let him redefine what it means to be a Republican and escape responsibility for an attack on the U.S. Capitol by a mob of his own supporters, mounted after he tried to overturn an election he lost. What his party offers voters this fall is him.

Republicans regrouped here for a midterm convention brought to life by Trump and for Trump, and that faithfulness was the point. They called him the greatest president in the nation’s history, thanked God for him winning again and even had the chance to buy a hat in his familiar shade of red saying he “was right about everything.”

“I don’t think we will ever — ever — have another president with this type of character, and I think it’s refreshing,” said Matt Long, a conservative Texas radio voice. “And I’ve loved every minute of it.” 

It was two days of Trump-tenored programming, a display honed since he beat a Bush, a Clinton and a field of governors and senators to first win the White House. The goal was to convince the country that Trump and his party should keep control of Congress — even though what’s happened in Washington is unrecognizable to allies of the last Republican president who came before him.

“They’re not even remotely close to conservative,” said Marc Racicot, the former Montana governor who led the Republican National Committee during George W. Bush’s first term and has turned to supporting several Democrats in recent years. “They’re mean, they’re suspicious of everything. They’re angry and bitter, and carnival barking usually is what they’re engaged in.”

Trump’s time on the political scene has been animated by those he deems an antagonist. First it was Barack Obama, whom he maligned with a racist falsehood in 2012. Then it was the Republican establishment in the 2016 primary, before he turned to Hillary Clinton and kept her from becoming the nation’s first woman president.

His defining rival may still be Joe Biden, Obama’s vice president, who ousted Trump from the White House in 2020, a loss so shocking to the president and his allies that they tried, and failed, to overturn it. Biden remains the only candidate of either party ever to beat Trump in a campaign. And even as Trump returned to power in 2024, chasing Biden from his re-election bid after a disastrous debate and then defeating Vice President Kamala Harris that fall, he never got the chance to defeat the man who had defeated him.

The party Biden led has spent the two years since asking how it lost to Trump again, after all it had done to center its strategy on running against him.

“Looking back in the history books, I hope that Trump is seen as one of the most divisive presidents our nation has ever seen, and that he should have never been re-elected in 2024,” said Jane Kleeb, a national Democratic party leader from Nebraska. “And obviously as Democrats, we have a responsibility that we own of allowing him to be re-elected, that we lost touch with so many voters that they lost faith in us as a party that they thought that he was the only hope to put more money in their pockets.”

Absent a main opponent this November, Republicans have gone looking for one. In this, they’ve taken two tacks. 

First, they’ve reached back to the last one. “To the American people, look: I know many of you are still struggling thanks to Joe Biden and the Democrats,” North Carolina Rep. Richard Hudson, the leader of the House Republican campaign arm, told the crowd. Visible during the convention were signs saying “Biden & Harris Broke It — Help Is On The Way.”

But it’s precisely the absence of Biden or any single defining leader that has left Democrats riven and opened room for a surge of democratic socialism among those who concluded that the party’s old blend of center-left and progressive ideas was no match for Trump. That, in turn, has given Republicans a foil, if not a lone foe — one they can describe as aberrant — and license to cast Trump as the only route to a prosperity they say is otherwise out of reach.

“To the American people listening, I say: If all you want out of life is what little these communists are offering, I guess that’s your right,” House GOP Majority Whip Tom Emmer told the audience in Texas. “Or you can join Donald J. Trump and Republicans, and have the opportunity to realize your greatest dreams, to achieve your greatest potential, to live free in the greatest country the world has ever known.”

Trump used his own turn onstage to ask the country to defy the gravity of a midterm year, when the president’s party is usually rebuked, and keep siding with him instead. On the convention’s first day, he promised a $5,000 dividend to every adult citizen if Republicans hold both chambers of Congress — a proposal with neither a plan to implement it nor accounting for how it would be paid for, let alone the ethical concerns it raises.

“You know what happens if you don’t vote? You go to hell,” Trump said on the second night of the convention, earning laughter from the arena. “You know that, okay? You go to hell, and I don’t want that to happen to you.”

Among his supporters, some come for the policy, and some for the bluster. The convention had its share of attendees in MAGA-coded red, white and blue, attracting the attention of cameras. It also had people who back him for the plainer reason that they believe he has made their lives better.

“He is probably a once-in-a-generation type of person. Love him or hate him, I love him, but you know the other side doesn’t,” said Laura McCravy Hunter, a South Carolina Republican. “It is impossible to say that he has not had an extreme impact on the party.”

Not every GOP candidate who will decide control of Congress came to Dallas. Some stayed home to keep the focus local, aware that Trump drives Republican passion but draws out opposing voters, too.

Stewart Rhodes, the Texas man whose sentence for his role in the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol was commuted almost as soon as Trump returned to office, made his way around the arena one evening this week. Rhodes, founder of the Oath Keepers, was found guilty of seditious conspiracy and sentenced to 18 years in prison before the president’s wide-ranging clemency for those convicted over that day.

Almost all the Republicans in Congress who tried to hold Trump accountable for the stolen-election falsehoods that led to the riot have since left office or lost.

Yet hours before Trump spoke in Dallas, there Rhodes was — a reminder of how the president has wielded his power, as Republicans ask voters to stick with them and the man they follow.

news.title: Assessing the headline hopefuls for Democrats in 2028
news.text:
With Democratic National Committee fundraising in the dumps and a fight for the soul of the party between centrists and progressives, will Dems snatch defeat from the jaws of victory in 2028? There is a dearth of potential candidates with national name-recognition and viability.

Republicans have their own issues. With Vice President J.D. Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio as current GOP frontrunners, they are beatable by a strong Democrat — presumably a centrist but conceivably from an emergent progressive wing. Vance’s “deal” with Iran wasn’t worth the napkin it was scrawled on, and Rubio’s experience in the Senate was forgotten when he allowed dismantling of USAID, leaving millions of African lives blowing in the wind.

President Donald Trump’s approval ratings are at an all-time low, comparable to Richard Nixon’s just before he resigned, making the GOP vulnerable in 2028. But there are real weaknesses to the four Democratic potential contenders currently riding double-digits: former Vice President Kamala Harris, U.S. Rep. Alexandria Octavio-Cortez, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and California Gov. Gavin Newsom. Harris: Just say no. An AOC candidacy rests on a progressive wave. Buttigieg would represent a significant breakthrough. Meanwhile, the most traditionally appealing of the four is Newsom; classically, he most fits the part. Remember, John F. Kennedy lost on radio and won on TV. So let’s look at Newsom’s record.

I’m a frequent visitor to San Francisco. Newsom’s abject failure during his time as mayor to provide an alternative to the unhoused being forced to use the sidewalks of his town as a public restroom inclined me to judge him ineffectual at best, a pretty boy at worst. That failure stands. The city’s current mayor, Daniel Lurie, seems to be taking meaningful steps in this regard. The jury is out, but it appears that if Newsom had the will, he hadn’t the way. Let’s give that subject a failing grade.

Lifting my gaze from the ground, Newsom’s record in office is a mixed bag with much to recommend him on the social issue front and some instances of crony capitalism that might be damning were it not that no one can compete with the current kleptocracy in Washington.

In terms of public health, beyond the derelict streets of San Francisco, the state’s reliance on some of the country’s most restrictive COVID-19 regulations was another black mark. As University of California San Francisco Professor of Medicine Monica Gandhi, among others, has noted, the governor’s edicts during the pandemic “did not lead to better health outcomes.” In Fox parlance, they smacked of “woke” agenda versus common sense.

On other social and cultural fronts — equally divisive but more defensible and, in several cases, ahead of their time — Newsom showed some spine and commendable proactivity. His California became a “sanctuary” for abortion rights for those fleeing neighboring states without access. He made assisted suicide legal. He did both of these as a practicing Catholic and without giving the pope any guff. Most admirably, as mayor, he fought the California Supreme Court to enable same-sex marriage, even violating state law at the time. You can say it was San Francisco, but he took the heat.

On the subject of the affordable housing crisis, to which I devoted a 2025 Eagle Reels vodcast with Patrick White of the Stockbridge Affordable Housing Trust, Newsom was responsible for loosening up zoning requirements in line with one of White’s key recommendations. In “not-in-my-backyard” California, handcuffed by 1978’s infamous Proposition 13 limiting property tax hikes for existing homeowners, Newsom helped enable duplex and fourplex construction where zoning had previously allowed exclusively single-family homes. This is a model for municipal planning in the Berkshires and elsewhere.

Beyond Newsom? Michelle Obama’s contention that we’re “not ready for a woman” and the Democratic strategist who told Axios “it has to be a white guy” have no supporting data. Hillary Clinton won the popular vote. Harris has old-line support. AOC represents a younger face of the party. Former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg has many fans, if voters look past sexual politics. Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel is a voice of reason, as is Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro; they are both Jewish, which some see as a liability; this might eventually hurt Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff as well, as he is also Jewish, but for now he is climbing in polling. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear has much to like.

Meanwhile, we sit in Casablanca and wait … and wait.

news.title: Meghan and Harry’s Cotswold life reveals a worrying truth about rural England
news.text:
Meghan and Harry, the Duchess and Duke of Sussex, have relocated to the UK as non-working royals and most interestingly, it’s believed that they are basing themselves in the Cotswolds, where they lived as newlyweds between 2018 and 2019. Parents at an unnamed private school in the area were contacted about new rules appearing to reference the Sussexes’ children. And then, last week came reports that Meghan had been spotted at Soho Farmhouse, an outpost of the exclusive private members’ club Soho House which functions as a luxury Cotswolds retreat.

But Meghan is only the latest American to set up life in the Cotswolds. Talk-show host Ellen DeGeneres moved there in 2024 with her wife, actress Portia Rossi, for a “simpler way of life”. She left her 43-acre estate after reportedly living in it for just a month, because it wasn’t big enough for Rossi’s horses. Taylor Swift supposedly rented a £3.3m property near Great Tew during her Eras tour in 2024, while Beyoncé and Jay Z have been spotted staying on a private estate in the area. Even A-listers who visit briefly, like Tom Cruise, frequent Soho Farmhouse. The English countryside has become a playground for rich Americans.

This exodus of wealthy Americans since Donald Trump’s re-election and a weakening of the pound has shaken up the local property market. Last year, Savills said the proportion of North Americans buying Cotswold properties above £1.5m quadrupled from its long-term average of 3.5 per cent to 13 per cent. In March, the Cotswolds office of The Buying Solution, an agency which specialises in properties over £2m, said they had already recorded a 50 per cent year-on-year increase in American clients since the start of this year.Sure, the Cotswolds has, to a degree, always been the playground of the rich and famous. In 2012 a network of high-profile individuals including the likes of David Cameron and broadcaster Jeremy Clarkson were crowned the “Chipping Norton set” because they had homes near the eponymous market town. But what is different now is the speed and scale of the influx of money into the area. In the past, the phenomenon of wealthy Londoners buying homes in the Cotswolds was not accompanied by so many news reports of it unsettling local people and dynamics.

In contrast, often the arrival of Americans is, perhaps characteristically, hard to miss. When JD Vance visited the Cotswolds a year ago, there was uproar after roads and footpaths were closed, residents had their vans searched by sniffer dogs, and a helipad was cut into a field. When Eve Jobs, daughter of the late Apple founder Steve Jobs, got married in the area last year, residents complained the countryside had been taken over by Secret Service agents due to the attendance of former US vice-president Kamala Harris.

The village of Bibury in Gloucester has imposed restrictions on coaches over the last year, after facing up to 20,000 visitors on busy weekends (it has a population of 600). When I visited the picturesque village of Castle Combe recently, I could barely see it through the crowds of visitors who, judging by their accents, were mostly American. Reporting from Business Insider found that at The Bull in Burford, a hotel and collection of restaurants, half the clientele are Americans, and they have imported a culture of tipping. Stores in the Cotswolds now stock American staples too – from Hershey’s chocolate to American pancake mix.

And sometimes the effects of outsiders taking over the Cotswolds unfold in ways that are not immediately obvious. A report prepared for Cotswold District Council in June lays bare fears that wealthier outsiders “out-compete local households” via second homes and holiday lets, thus restricting the supply of lower-cost properties. Fewer residents using local shops and services affects the “vitality and viability of local communities and service provision within them”. A friend whose family used to live in the South Cotswolds said their former family home was flipped by wealthy outsiders who then sold it at a price unaffordable for locals. They failed to get involved in the local community – which he says is “what life in a Cotswold village is all about”.

We talk plenty about Britain’s housing crisis, but much of the conversation in the media is confined to cities like London. What about the homelessness emergency that is playing out in rural communities? The number of county and rural households in temporary accommodation has increased by nearly 80 per cent over six years (much greater than the increase nationally and in London). The Cotswold District Council website explicitly lists in its priorities that “local people struggle to find and afford suitable accommodation, and many of the district’s younger generation are forced to leave the area because they can’t afford to live here”.

This looks especially perverse given an increase in second homes in the Cotswolds means around one in 10 properties are often vacant, according to the Office of National Statistics. Up to one in five homes in the parish of Swells, near Stow-on-the-Wold, are estimated to be holiday lets. Indeed, Meghan and Harry are reportedly keeping their home in Montecito, and also own a holiday property in Portugal. Will their Cotswold home be empty while they are at their other properties?

The Cotswolds aren’t the only bit of British countryside becoming overriden with the rich and famous, either. Burnham Market, a traditional Georgian village in Norfolk has been nicknamed “Chelsea-on-Sea” due to the influx of second homeowners from elsewhere. Villagers have complained that local essentials like the pharmacy and baker’s have been replaced by “posh gift shops”, and last year voted to ban existing homes from being turned into holiday retreats. Mawgan Porth, a rural settlement in Cornwall, has been nicknamed Hollywood-on-Sea after celebrities like Stanley Tucci, Cate Blanchett and Jason Momoa bought homes in the area. Local residents accused Blanchett in 2023 of a “land grab” and creating “constant misery” with her building work (Blanchett’s architects dismissed the idea the noise came from their clients’ property). 

Perhaps you can’t blame Americans for choosing to come here. For them the Cotswolds are “quaint”, or to borrow Kourtney Kardashian’s understated description of the area last year – a “dreamy storybook fairy tale”. The best bits of rural life are carefully packaged together: honey-coloured stone buildings, log fires, organic shops.

But it makes you wonder: who is the English countryside really for these days? We used to think of the countryside as being a nationwide inheritance; the National Trust’s mission is to “protect nature, beauty and history – for everyone”. But wealthy Americans are reimagining it as something to be experienced through gated estates and private clubs. Rural England is still being carefully preserved – but this time by people who can afford to keep others out. The Cotswolds is open to everyone, provided you can afford the membership fee.

news.title: 25 Years and America Still Stands Tall
news.text:
September 11, 2001, is one of those days in American history that will “live in infamy.” Just like the Japanese on December 7, 1941, who thought they could strike a mortal blow against the United States by their dastardly attack on Pearl Harbor, Osama bin Laden believed he could so weaken America, with his attack on multiple sites on the East Coast, that the country might never fully recover from it.

The Japanese were wrong in 1941 and found out, pretty quickly, that they were wrong. 

Osama bin Laden was wrong, too. Twenty-five years later, America is still the strongest nation in the world, with the most powerful military that can humble a nation using only a fraction of its power, and an economy that remains the envy of the world. Millions upon millions of people still migrate to America because America is…well, it’s America. The symbol of freedom, prosperity, and all that should be right in the world. We don’t mind immigrants coming to America; we only wish they’d come legally, as previous generations did, and become true Americans — not try to change the country into their image.

But the Japanese didn’t succeed in stopping America. Osama bin Laden didn’t succeed in humbling the country. And if the hate-America immigrants think they are going to do it, they’ve got a long, hard battle ahead of them.

America — true America — the land of the free, the home of the brave — a country “endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights, that among these are Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness”—this country is far from finished.

And the great people within it — which, sadly, is not all of them anymore — are not going to lay down, roll over, and show their belly for anybody. Not even other Americans.

For our greatest enemy in the world today is not outside our borders. Oh, we definitely must keep our eyes open and our powder dry regarding Communist China, Russia, and the Middle East; but those countries will never destroy America from without. Not unless or until we first destroy ourselves from within.

news.title: The tactics at 'Trump-a-palooza' reveal risks for Republicans
news.text:
The first thing I saw when I walked into "Trump-a-palooza" was Joe Biden.

The stadium screens were projecting his headshot, his eyes shooting red laser beams like a killer robot.

The use of the old meme came to represent two things about this week's Republican convention in Texas.

The first thing: even more than the event was about Trump, it was about Democrats.

On day one, at least, Biden and Kamala Harris kept flashing up on the screens as though we'd time-travelled to 2024.

And the second thing: the Republican messaging hasn't shifted a whole lot since Biden and Harris were in office.

This event featured the same scares as the 2024 convention: transgender athletes want to take over your daughters' sports leagues. Pro-vaccine doctors want to steal your power to decide what's best for your kids. Criminal illegal aliens might murder you during the night.

The most notable change to the talking points was how the adjectives had been amplified.

The "radical left lunatics" are now "crazy communists". Democrats are pursuing a "Bolshevik revolution" and want to "remake America in the image of every socialist hellscape of the last century".

Arguably, Trump's mistruths, as they are sometimes politely described, have been notched up too.

Separating real facts from "alternative facts" can get tricky when Trump speaks, but not always. There is something surreal about watching a speaker deliver a lengthy insistence that a venue is full while there are hundreds of unfilled seats around you.

"The highest rafter, no empty seats," Trump said, while actually pointing to entire sections of empty seats in the stadium's highest rafter.

Three topics proved taboo, except when Trump spoke

The headline from Trump's keynote address was an offer of free cash — a "Trump dividend", rather than a bribe, payable if voters vote the right way.

But his lengthy speech otherwise contained a lot of recycled material.

He told a familiar story about where "tariffs" fits on his list of favourite words. He recited a well-worn tale about being bullied by reporters over the price of eggs. And he reminded the crowd, no fewer than half a dozen times, that Iran must not have nuclear weapon.

Anyone who had listened to enough Trump rallies had heard it all before.

But it was notable that Trump chose to spend so much time on these three issues. Tariffs, affordability and Iran had largely been absent from the previous speeches.

They all rate highly among the list of factors contributing to Trump's poor approval rating, so other speakers largely steered clear of them.

One of Trump's most politically interesting choices was to speak dismissively about cost-of-living issues, and re-prosecute his old argument that the "affordability crisis" is "fake", but, in any case, he has solved it.

"Food prices and almost every other item are rapidly going down," he said.

"And by the way, oil will be going down as soon as we win the war with Iran, which is taking place right now."

Polls consistently show voters are not buying this message. In one recent poll, 69 per cent of respondents disapproved of Trump's handling of inflation and living costs, while just 17 per cent approved.

A telling conversation in a Texas park

So what was the point of the midterms convention spectacle?

What's the president's strategy when he insists that the affordability crisis is not a thing?

Why tell Americans, who keep complaining to pollsters they are struggling with rising prices, that "tariffs" remains a favourite word?

And for that matter, why speak at such length about the stadium being full? All that was ever guaranteed to do was spawn viral videos showing rows of empty seats and a man on stage insisting a lie is a truth.

The MAGA diehards in the arena were hyped. But away from it all, is there any chance that a parade-of-speeches event like this can move the midterms needle?

One of the most interesting people I met in Dallas was a Trump supporter who did not attend the convention. He was a long-time local named Daniel, who I chatted with in a city park.

"Personally, I love Trump," Daniel said. "He's the best president we've ever had. He's brought our economy back up. That's about all I've got to say about the good guy."

But when I asked if there was anything he didn't like, it turned out he did have more to say.

"A lot of them don't have papers, but they're part of Texas now."

Daniel revealed himself as one of those Trump voters who felt his mass deportation campaign had gone too far. His views were a long way from the narrative about "criminal illegal aliens" being pushed at the convention.

"It kind of brings a tear to my eye," Daniel continued.

"I can understand him doing his job and deporting the bad ones, but a lot of them are here just to provide for their family, you know. It really hurts."

Risks for Republicans

On issues ranging from immigration and Iran, and especially when it comes to living costs, some Trump supporters are seeing problems with their president.

The party is aware of this risk, and how Trump's "pretend I'm on the ballot" strategy could backfire in the midterms.

Vice-President JD Vance pleaded with those voters in his keynote address.

"Do not throw the baby out with the bathwater," he said. "Don't give the country over to a bunch of crazy people because you happen to disagree with us on a policy here or there."

While the party's messaging may not have changed a lot since 2024, circumstances have.

Trump's approval rating is at dire lows. But he has deliberately tied his party's fortunes to his own popularity, and he demonstrated his campaign strategy is not shifting.

The Republicans face a real risk of losing control of Congress in November's midterm elections.

Away from the stadium, those Americans who actually paid attention to "Trump-a-palooza" will likely be left wondering if it can improve the party's prospects at all.
news.summary: Donald Trump's approval rating is at dire lows. But he has deliberately tied his party's fortunes to his own popularity, and "Trump-a-palooza" showed his tactics are not changing.

news.title: Donald Trump lashes out at ABC News reporter Rachel Scott during tense exchange on Dallas airport tarmac
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has lashed out at an ABC News reporter on a Texas airport tarmac, repeatedly shutting down her questions as he prepared to leave Dallas.

The tense exchange unfolded on Thursday, September 10, as ABC News senior political correspondent Rachel Scott attempted to question Mr Trump about his pledge to give every American adult $US5000 if Republicans win the midterm elections.

“Not you, not you. Hey, not you,” Mr Trump, 80, said, wagging his finger at Scott, 33.

Mr Trump emphasised his final “not you” by stepping towards the journalist and leaning down in her direction before turning to take questions from other reporters.

ABC News has since publicly backed Scott following the confrontation.

“We wholeheartedly support Rachel Scott and our entire Washington team who do an exceptional job delivering trusted and straightforward reporting to the public every single day,” an ABC News spokesperson said in a statement.

Scott has not publicly addressed the incident beyond posting footage of the exchange on X alongside the caption, “My question to Trump tonight.”

It is far from the first heated exchange between Mr Trump and Scott, with the President repeatedly taking aim at the journalist and her reporting since returning to the White House.

During an appearance at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in May, Mr Trump turned towards a group of construction workers before describing Scott as “stupid,” “one of the worst reporters” and “a horror show.”

The President also declared her questions were “a disgrace to our country” after she questioned him about his focus on projects in Washington DC while the US was at war with Iran and Americans faced rising petrol prices.

The White House later shared footage of that exchange on X with the caption, “@POTUS destroys ABC Fake News reporter.”

Another fiery encounter unfolded during a White House Cabinet meeting in December 2025, when Scott questioned Mr Trump over US airstrikes on boats off the coast of Venezuela that his administration accused of carrying drugs.

“You are the most obnoxious reporter in the whole place,” Trump said when Scott asked if he would commit to releasing the full video of a recent strike that triggered allegations it could qualify as a war crime. “Let me just tell you, you are an obnoxious — a terrible reporter.”

Separate analyses by The New York Times and London-based nonprofit Airwars found US strikes in the region had killed at least 227 people during the past 12 months, none of whom had been formally charged with a crime.

The pair’s history of tense exchanges stretches back to Mr Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign.

During an appearance at the National Association of Black Journalists convention, Scott asked Mr Trump “why should Black voters trust you”.

“I don’t think I’ve ever been asked a question in such a horrible manner,” he responded.

“I think it’s disgraceful that I came here in good spirit. I love the Black population of this country, I’ve done so much for the Black population of this country,” he replied.

Later during the July 2024 interview, Mr Trump questioned whether then-Vice President Kamala Harris was really Black.

Mr Trump’s clashes with female journalists have also extended beyond Scott, with the White House forced to defend his language towards reporters in November 2025.

That month, the President described New York Times reporter Katie Rogers as “ugly, both inside and out” and snapped, “Quiet. Quiet, Piggy” at Bloomberg correspondent Catherine Lucey aboard Air Force One.

“Look, the president is very frank and honest with everyone in this room,” then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said in defense of Trump’s “piggy” remark. “I think everyone in this room should appreciate the frankness and the openness that you get from President Trump on a near-daily basis.”

Mr Trump has also repeatedly clashed with CNN’s Kaitlan Collins and New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman.

The President has taken to calling Haberman “Maggot” and on Tuesday, September 8, described her as “unattractive, both inside and out”.

The New York Times hit back the following day, accusing the President of attacking journalists over reporting he does not like.

“This is another all too common example of the president lashing out at coverage he doesn’t like and belittling journalists who report the facts,” the Times said in a statement on Wednesday, Sept. 9.
news.summary: US President Donald Trump has been caught in a tense confrontation with a female reporter after lunging towards her and shutting down her question.
news.author: Madeline Cove

news.title: The GOP was confident about keeping its Senate majority. Now the fight for control is wide open
news.text:
WASHINGTON — Republicans appeared to have a firm grip on the Senate heading into the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term. But with less than two months until Election Day, control of the chamber is now up for grabs.

Democrats have found themselves competing in states that once seemed beyond their reach as Trump’s slipping approval ratings and voters’ dissatisfaction with the economy create a difficult political environment for Republicans. But races Democrats once counted on winning have also become more complicated.

It’s a battle that’s expected to exceed $3.4 billion in spending across all races during the midterm campaign. The implications are huge for Trump’s agenda and his ability to fill administration jobs and open court seats for the remainder of his term, as the Senate is empowered to confirm or block presidential nominees.

Republicans say it’s unlikely for everything to break in Democrats’ favor, but they acknowledge they’re facing a difficult landscape. Senate Majority Leader John Thune told South Dakota’s KELOLAND News last week that he does “worry” about losing the chamber.

“I’m a realist,” Thune said. “I don’t ever try and sugarcoat things. I think it’s a competitive environment right now.”

Democrats face a scrambled path to the majority

Democrats need to net four seats to win the majority. The original path had been to hold Michigan, Georgia and New Hampshire while winning back Republican-held seats in Alaska, Maine, North Carolina and Ohio. But things have changed.

“We now have multiple paths for the majority,” Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said last month. “We found new states — Iowa, Texas — which people a year ago weren’t even paying attention to.”

Some of the states where Democrats were feeling most optimistic at the start of the election cycle, such as Michigan and Maine, have grown murkier.

In Michigan, where there’s an open seat this fall, no GOP candidate has won a Senate race since 1994. But Democrats are struggling to unite behind nominee Abdul El-Sayed. The favorite of progressives narrowly defeated moderate U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens in the August primary, and feelings remain raw from a bruising contest that saw nearly $70 million spent against El-Sayed.

Republicans believe Mike Rogers, who lost the 2024 Senate race by fewer than 20,000 votes, has an improved shot against El-Sayed. The Senate Leadership Fund — Senate Republicans’ spending PAC — added $6 million to its Michigan advertising investment after El-Sayed won, bringing their total spending to $51 million, the third-highest total.

Democrats also saw a prime opportunity to finally defeat five-term Republican Sen. Susan Collins in Maine, where Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris won more votes than Trump in 2024.

Progressive Graham Platner easily won the nomination in June, but he left the race the next month over a sexual assault allegation that he denies. Democratic delegates in late July chose Troy Jackson, a lesser-known former state legislative leader, to replace him.

Jackson has been forced to play catch-up. Collins and aligned super PACs have spent almost $80 million so far, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact, while Jackson and Democratic-aligned groups have spent and reserved close to $45 million since he became the nominee.

As one path narrowed for Democrats, others widened

Democrats increasingly see a real possibility in Texas, a state that has been an elusive goal for decades, and other GOP-led states including Iowa, Alaska and Ohio.

In Texas, Democrat James Talarico faces state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who ousted four-term incumbent Republican Sen. John Cornyn to win the GOP nomination. Senate GOP leadership backed Cornyn, seeing him as the stronger general election candidate.

Paxton has been shadowed for decades by legal and ethical questions, including indictments for securities fraud, though he was not convicted.

Talarico and allied groups have spent nearly $30 million on advertising since the May runoff, compared to less than $3 million by pro-Paxton groups. The political fund associated with Trump last week spent $10 million on TV and digital ads to help Paxton — the first major general election investment by MAGA Inc. for the midterms. Senate GOP leaders had petitioned Trump’s political team to spend some of the more than $400 million it had last month to help Paxton.

Democrats have also upped their spending in Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and North Carolina, all states currently held by Republicans. The GOP, meanwhile, is feeling more optimistic about New Hampshire as well as Michigan, while spending more to defend seats in Iowa and Alaska.

The expanded map has upped the anticipated total spending this cycle. AdImpact in June projected $3.4 billion in advertising spending on Senate races, a significant increase from the $2.8 billion the ad spending firm projected in the fall of 2025.

Why more states are in play than expected

Democrats’ path has widened in part because of Trump’s slumping job approval, notably on handling the economy, which was at 32 percent according to an AP-NORC poll in July — down from 40 percent in March 2025, shortly after he took office.

Trump’s trade policies and the war in Iran, with its corresponding inflated fuel costs, have added to the economic uncertainty for voters less than two months before Election Day.

“Things still cost too much. And so we’ve got to work on that issue,” Republican Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio told The Associated Press. “We understand that and we know that’s real.”

Ohio Sen. Jon Husted heard the concern firsthand at a roundtable last month. Husted is looking to fend off a comeback from former Sen. Sherrod Brown in another key matchup for both parties.

During the discussion on housing, one attendee told Husted that costs were “skyrocketing” in part because of uncertainty around tariffs.

“Uncertainty is the killer to this economy,” said Dean Windham, a real estate developer who previously ran for office as a Republican.

Some Republican Senate candidates have defended Trump’s policies while confronting concerns about their economic impact.

In Michigan, where Trump’s tariffs on Canada have become a central issue, Rogers has backed the president’s approach while leaving room for disagreement.

“President Trump is right to put America First — and tariffs are necessary, but are not a one-size-fits-all solution,” Rogers said in a recent statement.

Republicans believe the math still favors them

Even if Democrats hold every seat they currently control, they would need to flip at least two seats in states Trump carried by double digits in 2024 to win the majority.

Republicans are betting that those underlying advantages will matter more as Election Day approaches — particularly as Trump and the party turn their attention toward mobilizing voters who helped return him to the White House.

Trump told reporters last week that he will “be making a lot of stops” in the last 30 days before the election.

This week, Republicans will hold a midterm convention in Texas, where Trump is set to speak and top Senate candidates including Rogers and Husted are expected to attend.

But Republicans acknowledge they have work to do.

“Politics is local,” Republican Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota said. He pointed to Trump’s decision to import beef, which he said made farmers and ranchers “feel just like the administration pulled the rug right off from underneath” them.

“They’re hurt,” Rounds said. “They feel like they’ve been let down.”
news.summary: WASHINGTON — Republicans appeared to have a firm grip on the Senate heading into the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term. But with less than two months until Election Day, control of the chamber is now up for…

news.title: Maine Democrat Troy Jackson Tours ‘Inclusive’ Welding School with Zero Tolerance for ‘Fatphobia’
news.text:
Maine Democrat U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson visited People’s Inclusive Welding in South Portland during a Labor Day weekend tour, praising the school’s emphasis on inclusion and pledging support for apprenticeship programs like it.

WGME reported that Jackson stopped at the hands-on welding training facility on Saturday as part of a Labor Day weekend tour to meet working Mainers.

“Making people feel included is how we are going to do a lot better across this state and country,” Jackson told the outlet.

People’s Inclusive Welding shop owner Jo Remillard told WGME, “A lot of funding has been pulled for workforce training, especially because our school has ‘inclusive’ in the name, that can disqualify us from federal funding, and you know, we are creating skilled trades workers who are going to work on Maine’s infrastructure.”

“Apprenticeship programs like this is something I’ve always supported. I am certainly going to support more money and support into this if I am lucky enough to pull this off,” Jackson said.

People’s Inclusive Welding states that its mission is to provide “a safe and supportive environment for underserved and underrepresented communities” to complete welding training and receive workers’ rights education so they can enter “a high paying career within the blue collar industry.”

The school’s handbook says PIW seeks relationships with employers that practice racial sensitivity training and wants every student to have “an equitable chance at receiving every ounce of education that they desire within their chosen course.”

The handbook also tells students that school can be “a triggering and anxiety-inducing space for many people” and asks them to practice kindness and patience with their peers and themselves.

PIW’s handbook lists “fatphobia” among conduct prohibited under its zero-tolerance policy for discrimination, harassment, and violence, alongside “racism, sexism, ableism, homophobia, transphobia, xenophobia, islamophobia, fatphobia, antisemitism, or any other form of discrimination.” Although the handbook says the policy is “as outlined under Maine Law,” the Maine Human Rights Commission’s list of protected classes does not separately include “fatphobia” or weight as a protected status.

PIW further states that it “is committed to anti-racism” and that both “over-expressions and microaggressions will be taken seriously.” The handbook adds, “Under no circumstances will the police be called or be allowed into the shop space.”

Remillard says being the only “femme” in many workplaces prompted questions about representation in the trades.

“As I grew older, my acceptance of this reality dissipated and I began to ask myself why there weren’t more women, people of color, or immigrants? Where are the Indigenous people? Folks with disabilities? Or anyone from the gay community?! Even if there were 1 or 2 people from these groups, why did they hold the less skilled, lower paying jobs?” Remillard states on PIW’s website.

Remillard said the murder of George Floyd led to becoming “a student of anti-racism” and to realizing that “the position I held in my career was given to me through the inequitable advantages and privilege every white person is granted via systemic white supremacy.”

PIW board member Arlo Hennessey, who identifies as “a black trans man with mixed heritage,” states, “I know the trades have a racism and inclusion issue.”

Hennessey said “safe and good paying union jobs are prohibited through gate keeping,” which keeps “otherwise qualified black, indigenous, immigrants, poc, and lgbtqia+ people from ever making it in the door.”

“If they make it that far they have to work twice as hard with twice the harassment just to prove themselves,” Hennessey added.

“Black, indigenous, immigrant, poc, and lgbtqia+ people are going to have a seat at the table, or these industries are gonna die,” Hennessey states.

Jackson’s stop at the school comes as the former Maine Senate president campaigns against incumbent Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME). He has been endorsed by former vice president and failed presidential candidate Kamala Harris.

Jackson became Maine Democrats’ U.S. Senate nominee at the party’s July 25 convention, replacing Graham Platner who withdrew after a former girlfriend accused him of sexual assault, an allegation Platner denied.

Jackson has since faced scrutiny over a Washington Post report alleging he repeatedly yelled and cursed at fellow lawmakers, including during a 2021 dispute in which he threw a water bottle, as well as a 1988 assault case in which he has acknowledged punching a man. A police report from the incident also says longtime partner Lana Pelletier told an officer Jackson had “pushed her around,” though both Jackson and Pelletier now deny that he was violent toward her. Jackson and Pelletier have also been reported to be second cousins who share two children.

Jackson’s legislative record has also drawn attention. In 2023, he voted for legislation allowing some 16- and 17-year-olds to obtain nonsurgical gender-affirming hormone therapy without parental consent under specified conditions, supported taxpayer funding for transgender surgeries involving minors, and voted against several measures intended to protect girls’ sports. He also helped advance legislation that made Maine the first state to decriminalize selling sex and recently described himself as “working class” after Sen. Susan Collins said he had become “essentially a democratic socialist.”

Maine Democrat U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson visited People’s Inclusive Welding in South Portland during a Labor Day weekend tour, praising the school’s emphasis on inclusion and pledging support for apprenticeship programs like it.
