news.title: Democrat Rob Sand Double Digits Ahead in State Trump Won Three Times: Poll
news.text: Democrat Rob Sand led Republican Zach Lahn by 10 points among likely voters in a new poll of the governor’s race in Iowa, a state President Donald Trump won in each of his three presidential bids. Although Iowa has shifted rightward over the past decade, Democrats are hopeful about their prospects in the Hawkeye State this November. Sand, the current state auditor, has built a steady polling lead over Lahn, a businessman, and forecasters have shifted the race toward Democrats in the past few weeks. Iowa backed President Barack Obama in 2008 and 2012, but it voted for Trump in 2016, 2020 and 2024, giving him a 13-point victory in 2024, a sign that the once-purple state could be drifting away from competitive territory. Sand’s candidacy will gauge whether Democrats can make a comeback in the state, particularly among the white, working-class voters who voted for Obama before casting their ballots for Trump. Rob Sand Leads Zach Lahn in New Poll The new poll showed Sand up by 10 percentage points among likely voters, 51 percent to 41 percent. But he led by 11 points among all registered voters, 50 percent to 39 percent. His lead in the poll was bolstered by his ability to win over some voters who cast their ballots for Trump in 2024 while also holding together the Democratic Party. He won 97 percent of Vice President Kamala Harris’ 2024 voters, with only 1 percent of them backing Lahn. Among Trump voters, however, Sand won 12 percent to Lahn’s 73 percent. This suggests that some Trump voters are breaking Republican ranks to support the Democratic candidate. Harris voters also said they were more motivated to vote—94 percent said they would definitely vote, compared to 90 percent of Trump voters. The poll also found that the president is broadly unpopular in Iowa despite his past victories. Forty-one percent of Iowa respondents said they approved of Trump, compared to 57 percent who said they disapproved of him, the poll found. It surveyed 2,169 registered voters, 2,043 of whom were classified as “strict” likely voters, from September 3-8. The poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percent among registered voters and the likely voter subset. Lahn Campaign Responds The poll’s sample included 38 percent of respondents who have at least a bachelor’s degree, compared to 31 percent of Iowans overall with at least a bachelor’s degree, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. A Lahn spokesperson told Newsweek on Friday that the poll is “not a reliable source.” “Rob has spent over $7 million to go backwards in the polls. Iowans are realizing he’s a radical liberal who supports amnesty and government benefits for illegal aliens, no limits on abortion, AOC’s green new deal, and wants to raise taxes on Iowa families by $7,500 per year,” the spokesperson said. Newsweek also reached out to the Sand campaign for comment via email. What Other Polls Show Several other recent polls have shown Sand with a lead. A recent poll from Emerson College showed him with a 3-point lead, 49 percent to 46 percent. It surveyed 750 likely voters from August 31-September 1, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points. Sand also led the latest poll from Suffolk University, 48 percent to 44 percent, which polled 500 likely voters from August 20-23. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. Sand’s lead was tighter in a poll by The New York Times and Siena University, which showed him up only about a single point, 48 percent to 47 percent. It polled 600 likely voters from June 15-27. In a Fox News poll, Sand led by 9 points, 53 percent to 44 percent. It surveyed 1,003 registered voters from June 23-27 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. What Prediction Markets Show Sand is up in prediction markets, as well, having a 78 percent chance of victory on Kalshi and a 77 percent chance on Polymarket as of Friday afternoon. Prediction markets let traders buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real-money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always predict the future accurately. Why Democrats Believe Iowa Can Flip in 2026 Iowa was once a battleground that voted for politicians of both major parties but has steadily become a Republican stronghold in the Trump era. Obama won the state by about 10 points in 2008 and 6 points in 2012. But Trump performed well in the state, winning by 10 points in 2016, 8 points in 2020 and 13 points in 2024. Democrats have lost ground across the Midwest, as white working-class voters have shifted to Trump and Republicans. Any Democrat hoping to win Iowa must perform better among those voters. However, Democrats believe they may be able to make inroads with some voters in the midterms as Trump’s national approval rating falls due to economic concerns around the cost of living and inflation, as well as the unpopular war in Iran that has sent gas prices surging. Trump’s tariffs could also become a major issue in Iowa, home to many farmers who could be impacted by the policies. In addition to the gubernatorial race, Democrats are also hoping to compete in the U.S. Senate race, where GOP Senator Joni Ernst has opted to not run for reelection. Republican Representative Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Representative Josh Turek are running to succeed Ernst. Three of Iowa’s four congressional districts are viewed as competitive in the midterms as Democrats hope to reclaim a majority in the House. In Iowa’s First District, GOP Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks faces a rematch against Democrat Christina Bohannan, a former state representative who nearly unseated the Republican in 2024. In Iowa’s Second District, vacated by Hinson, Republican former state Representative Joe Mitchell and Democratic state Representative Lindsay James are running. In Iowa’s Third District, Representative Zach Nunn, a Republican, faces a challenge from Democratic state Senator Sarah Trone Garriott. Rob Sand Breaks From National Party Sand has sought to cast himself as an independent voice, breaking from the national party on some cultural issues. The strategy may be necessary in Iowa, where only 31 percent of respondents in the YouGov poll reported favorable views of Democrats, while 57 percent said they viewed the party unfavorably. The GOP was less unpopular, with 39 percent viewing the party favorably, though 53 percent still said they viewed the Republican Party unfavorably. Sand has broken with some of the more left-leaning members of his party on the issue of transgender athletes’ participation in women's and girls’ sports teams. “Everybody gets hard on the language. They get mad if you use this word or that word. I just think girls’ sports are for girls, and boys’ sports are for boys. I think that’s fair and reasonable,” he said. “At the same time, look, I respect a woman’s right to choose and reproductive freedom. If you want to get a gay marriage, help yourself.” What Happens Next The race is expected to be one of the most competitive of the midterms. The Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball both classify it as Leans Democratic, meaning it is competitive but that Sand has a slight advantage. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: Democrats believe they can flip Iowa, a state that backed Trump by double digits in 2024, in this year's midterms.

news.title: JD Vance Just Passed His 2028 Audition With Flying Colors
news.text:
JD Vance was a luxury pick. 

At least, that was the political consensus in 2024: He didn’t put any swing states in play, nor would he threaten a vital, must-win Democratic voting demo — like Latinos, women, or blacks. 

In fact, he didn’t change the political map at all. 

Hey, Ohio and/or rust-belt white dudes were voting for Trump anyway, so why shoulder-tap Ohio’s 39-year-old junior senator? Wouldn’t the GOP get more bang-for-the-buck with a different running mate?

But Vance was more than a luxury pick: He was also a legacy pick.

At the time, I compared it to talent projection in the NFL Draft:

The basic argument comes down to ceiling versus basements. A player with a high ceiling is a kid with untapped potential who might be a superstar, but still carries developmental risk; a player with a high basement is someone who can at least be an okay backup and hopefully an acceptable starter, but might not have the physical traits to develop any further.JD Vance was a high ceiling pick. He was selected for his upside.Other potential VPs had much higher basements. Tim Scott and Marco Rubio, for example, could be plugged in right away and potentially put the Left on the defensive, especially with key demographics that the Democrats desperately need to win. And someone like Nikki Haley could’ve contributed ASAP by peeling away women voters. JD Vance isn’t a plug-and-play VP selection. He’s mostly unknown to the American people, which means he’ll have to build his own profile and name recognition.

And what an upside! 

We saw our first glimpse of it when he utterly annihilated Kamala Harris’ “safe, experienced” pick of Gov. Tim Walz (D-Minn.) in their vice-presidential debate. It was such a thorough ass-kicking that Kamala Harris wrote in her memoir that she moaned out loud and barked advice at her TV.

From Fox News:

Harris mentioned a "Saturday Night Live" skit after the debate that depicted Harris and her husband Doug watching the debate and spitting out wine in shock. Harris wrote that while she did not actually spit out wine while watching, "it was otherwise uncanny in its portrait of our evening."

But after Trump-Vance rolled to a landslide victory, our story began to change. Vance did what all vice presidents do: He faded into the background, ceding the limelight to the president.

The benefit of the vice presidency is that it positions the titleholder as the heir apparent. Once your boss is term-limited, all eyes are on you.

The downside is, you’re the second banana for (at least) four years, subservient to the president. You’re the supporting actor, not the superstar — the B-side to a smash-hit single — and that carries a perceptual cost.

George H. W. Bush was a World War II veteran: the Navy’s youngest pilot and an honest-to-God war hero. But after eight years as vice president, the mainstream media called him a wimp.

The combination of President Ronald Reagan’s swagger, Bush’s gentlemanly demeanor, and the stigma of the vice presidency created this “wimp” PR problem. (Until Bush was bailed out by Dan Rather’s arrogance and condescension, showing his backbone on live TV.) 

Until now, Vance was being dragged down by the office, too.

The MAGAverse hasn’t seen Vice President Vance blasting Dems and brutalizing libs lately. Our Millennial messenger from Appalachia had mostly vanished from the periphery, popping up intermittently to chastise Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in an infamous Oval Office meeting, or negotiating a poorly received (and since failed) Memo of Understanding with Iran.

Meanwhile, Secretary of State Marco Rubio was moving mountains in the Americas, becoming Trump’s most popular cabinet pick. Gov. Ron DeSantis (R-Fla.) was finishing the most successful two-term governorship in U.S. history. Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Tex.) was battling Tucker Carlson for the soul of the conservative movement. Newer, younger MAGA superstars like Brandon Gill, Karoline Leavitt, and Anna Paulina Luna burst on the scene, rapidly building national profiles of their own. 

By comparison, Vance’s post-2024 narrative was kind of boring.

But it was more than that: Vance’s youth and inexperience made him a “blank slate,” because nobody was entirely sure where, exactly, he fit in the political spectrum.

Was he a classic conservative like Ted Cruz? A libertarian like Rand Paul? An America First interventionist like Marco Rubio? An obstructionist like Thomas Massie? An in-your-face leader like Ron DeSantis? A wackaloon like Tucker Carlson?

Is he a pragmatist, a nationalist, an incrementalist, or an ideologue? (Or, perhaps, a combination of all the above?)

Usually, the vice president is considered an extension of the president — but President Trump is such a sui generis, once-in-a-millennium personality, it’s unfathomable that anyone could be the “next” Donald Trump. He’s in a category all by himself.

Even if he wanted to, Vance couldn’t imitate Trump. Nobody can.

Which put the MAGAverse in the uncomfortable position of guessing what Vance really, truly believes. He became a Rorschach inkblot test, where audiences projected their own beliefs — and, alas, their own biases — on everything Vance said and did.

And that’s a perfectly viable PR strategy, by the way. Sometimes, by keeping your big mouth closed and projecting a happy, pleasant, friendly demeanor, you sidestep landmines and build bridges of friendship. (Dolly Parton was a master at it.)

But for the strategy to work, you’ve got to stick like Velcro to the plan. You can’t waver. Because, once you start feeding breadcrumbs to one side, the strategy doesn’t just fail — it spectacularly backfires.

People then assume your breadcrumbs aren’t breadcrumbs: They’re damning evidence of a deep-rooted bias that’s bubbling to the surface. 

It’s something you feel so strongly, you can’t help but reveal it. This is who you actually are.

And that scares the hell out of the other side!

There’s an internecine underway. At stake is the future of the MAGA movement. The Iran War exacerbated the fault lines, but truthfully? They were already there. 

At one extreme are the war hawks, internationalists, and neocons. At the other extreme are the conspiracy-pushing, pro-Islamic non-interventionists. Somewhere in the middle are legitimate debates over Israel, foreign policy, the dangers of Islam, and how we define American exceptionalism.

When Vance began criticizing Israel, lambasting neocons, pushing the MOU, and refusing to separate himself from his “friend” Tucker Carlson, his popularity in the GOP began to plummet. In the eyes of many in the MAGAverse, he chose the wrong side — and thus failed the Rorschach test.

And suddenly, the heir apparent wasn’t so apparent.

Is Marco Rubio now the GOP frontrunner? https://t.co/3cfqqhp5qe pic.twitter.com/zGWzLEUot9— Bloomberg (@business) February 22, 2016

🚨🇺🇸 Polymarket just put Marco Rubio ahead of JD Vance for the first time, making him the most likely man to become president in 2028.Source: @Polymarket / Writer: Mhedi pic.twitter.com/YEbONdAt2w— Mario Nawfal (@MarioNawfal) June 8, 2026

That’s not to say Vance was unloved by the base. His verbal shish kabobing of Tim Walz was still fondly remembered, and we still gave his boss the benefit of the doubt: If he’s good enough for Trump, he’s good enough for me, I guess.

But the luster was gone. Noticeable cracks had emerged. And like it or not, the anti-Vance whisper campaign was now fully underway. 

This was the backdrop of Vice President Vance’s RNC speech last night. Other than Trump, no one in America had more personally on the line.

It was Vance's 2028 audition test. If his speech was a dud, the whisper campaign would stop whispering — and start shouting.

Newsflash: Vance passed the test with flying colors.

RFK Jr. also gave a great speech, but the medium makes the message, and Kennedy’s voice, unfortunately, sounds like a lawnmower. (If RFK Jr. sounded like James Earl Jones, he’d be a helluva candidate in 2028!) And President Trump, of course, took the stage immediately afterwards, inviting comparisons between the status quo and the Next Big Thing.

On Thursday night, Vance outshone his boss, giving the better, more impressive speech.

He was charming and folksy. Family-friendly and introspective. Spontaneous and clever. And good Lord, he dissected the Democratic Party with surgical precision.

His most viral moment was how he made mincemeat of RNC protesters. Vance’s off-the-cuff response was textbook Trump:

.@VP in Dallas: "We just had a protestor interrupting us and waving the Mexican flag. Well, my friend, if you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there — I'll buy you the plane ticket." pic.twitter.com/PYkqtkLz6q— Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) September 11, 2026

But for political purposes, this moment mattered more:

🚨 JUST NOW: JD Vance drops this message to Americans and young men who are pessimistic about the direction of America"Don't give the country over to a bunch of CRAZY people because you disagree with us on a policy issue here or there!""Charlie Kirk had his own views. HE did… pic.twitter.com/xZ7oXTSYKs— Eric Daugherty (@EricLDaugh) September 11, 2026

Vance used his standing as Carlson’s friend to make an impassioned argument for GOP unity. Had he already excommunicated Carlson and his ilk, his message wouldn’t have had the same impact.

Which resets the Rorschach inkblot test: Instead of biting his tongue because he secretly agreed with Tucker Carlson, perhaps he’s biting his tongue because it’s the best way for Republicans to win.

Axios: Vance: MAGA’s Millennial Messenger for the Midterms

Support for President Trump is dropping among millennials and Gen Zers — particularly young men. Vice President Vance is in charge of getting them back in the midterms.Why it matters: The 42-year-old Vance, the first millennial VP, capped off the GOP's two-day convention here with a direct appeal to families with young children that emphasized the "birthright" of U.S. citizens.Vance also sought to cast Democrats as anti-American, anti-family "crazies.""America belongs to those who love it. Not those who hate it," he said.[…]Friction point: Vance obliquely touched on the major source of the administration's unpopularity — Trump's war in Iran and the high prices it's caused — and asked undecided and unsure voters to overlook it."I'm asking you to do what Charlie did: Do not throw the baby out with the bathwater."

Vance leveraged his age, family, and anti-war credibility to bridge internal divisions. He electrified MAGA’s base, welcomed back wayward voters, and gleefully filleted left-wing sacred cows.

Like James Talarico:

🔥🚨 JUST IN — JD Vance just absolutely DESTROYED Democrat James Talarico:"I gotta say, a guy that age who is so obsessed and focused on Transgender children- I don’t know about you, but I NEVER wanna see that guy’s web browser history!""This Talarico guy, he won’t shut up… pic.twitter.com/mx9k3QEHQQ— The Patriot Oasis™ (@ThePatriotOasis) September 11, 2026

And Abdul El-Sayed:

Vice President JD Vance DOG-WALKS Democratic Michigan U.S. Senate Candidate Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed: “[Abdul El-Sayed] saw me talking about my papaw… [and] asked mockingly, whether I'd be willing to bring Usha back in time to meet papaw. This is what he thinks of my… pic.twitter.com/5ey2q1fP6O— RedWave Press (@RedWavePress) September 11, 2026

And today’s Democratic Party:

🔥🚨 BREAKING — JD Vance just went on a RAMPAGE towards the radical Anti-American Democrat Party:"The Democrats are the party of HATERD!""Who the Democrats are now, my friends. They’re not just the party of a little higher taxes, maybe some dumb regulations.""They’re not… pic.twitter.com/Xr6JyV74Df— The Patriot Oasis™ (@ThePatriotOasis) September 11, 2026

Which led to the inevitable “JD 48” chant:

Woman in the crowd yells "JD 48"The crowd then breaks out into a "48" chant pic.twitter.com/1U6I9V7GnD— Townhall.com (@townhallcom) September 11, 2026

That’ll wait ‘til 2028. Today, there’s a midterm election to win.

But win or lose, Vice President Vance just took an enormous step forward. His rollicking RNC speech reminded the MAGAverse what makes him such a special candidate. His voice, his message, his sensibilities: It was all unmistakably JD — in the best possible way.

The 2028 race isn’t over. You’re not gonna win the 2028 nomination with a single 2026 speech. That’s unrealistic.

There’ll be more twists, turns, trials, and tribulations. There always are.

But something politically significant just happened: Vance is looking like the legacy pick we all hoped he would be.

And that’s a big freaking deal.

news.title: Peggy Flanagan's Chances of Losing to Michele Tafoya in Minnesota: Polls
news.text: Democratic Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan holds a narrow lead over Republican Michele Tafoya in Minnesota's U.S. Senate race, according to a new poll, though her advantage falls within the survey's margin of error, highlighting a competitive contest less than two months before Election Day on November 3. The poll comes as Democrats eye a narrow path to reclaiming control of Congress' upper chamber, where Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority. To take back the majority, Democrats must defend their current seats—including in two states President Donald Trump won in his 2024 White House bid—and flip four others. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party historically loses seats. The Cook Political Report currently rates the Minnesota Senate race as likely Democrat. Newsweek has reached out to the Flanagan and Tafoya campaigns for comment via email on Friday. Minnesota Senate Race Flanagan and Tafoya are vying for the seat held by Democrat Tina Smith, who is retiring. Minnesota last elected a Republican senator in 2002, backing Norm Coleman. In 2008, he lost reelection to Democrat Al Franken. Flanagan defeated Representative Angie Craig in the primary in August in a victory for the Democratic Party’s more progressive wing, which has seen several candidates prevail in recent primaries. Flanagan received backing from independent Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders and Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar, making the race another example of the ongoing divide between progressive and moderate Democrats. Tafoya, a former longtime NFL sideline reporter, won the Republican nomination and is seeking to turn her name recognition and political outsider profile into a victory. The race has drawn national attention as Republicans look to make gains in Minnesota, even though Democrats have maintained a strong statewide advantage in recent elections. Cook Political Report shifted the race from Lean Democrat to Likely Democrat in August. Vice President Kamala Harris, whose running mate was Minnesota Governor Tim Walz, won the state by roughly 4 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election over President Donald Trump. In 2016, Minnesota backed former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton by less than 2 percentage points against Trump. President Barack Obama did better in the state, carrying it by nearly 8 points in 2012 and more than 10 points in 2008. The North Star State became the epicenter of the Trump administration’s ramped-up immigration enforcement earlier this year. Two American citizens, Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti, were fatally shot by federal immigration officers in January amid protests in Minneapolis, fueling anger over the White House's hardline approach to immigration, border security and Operation Metro Surge. The state has also been in the national spotlight in recent months over fraud investigations. Minnesota Senate Race: Latest Poll A new Quantus Insights poll found Flanagan leading the race, 48.2 percent to Tafoya’s 44.4 percent. About 88.6 percent of participants said they are “definitely decided” about their vote, while 7.5 percent said they could be open to changing their mind. Women favored Flanagan by a 14-point margin, 54 percent to 40 percent, while men backed Tafoya by 8 points, 50 percent to 42 percent, according to the poll. The poll revealed a clear age divide. Flanagan led among voters under 45, winning support from 62 percent of those ages 18 to 29 compared with 28 percent for Tafoya, and from 63 percent of voters ages 30 to 44 compared with 34 percent for the Republican. Tafoya, meanwhile, led among older voters, 54 percent to 38 percent among those ages 45 to 64 and 47 percent to 44 percent among voters 65 and older. The poll found Flanagan with a 50 percent favorable rating and a 46 percent unfavorable rating. Tafoya was viewed favorably by 42.4 percent of respondents and unfavorably by 42 percent. The poll of 720 likely voters was conducted September 8-10 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.2 percentage points. What Other Polls Show The limited public polling conducted since the primary has generally shown Flanagan ahead of Tafoya, though some surveys have found a race that remains within the margin of error. A recent TIPP/League of American Workers poll, conducted August 31-September 2 among 1,201 likely voters, found Flanagan holding a narrow lead, 44 percent to 42 percent. It also found 6 percent supporting other candidates, while 8 percent were not sure. According to the poll, Flanagan had more of the Gen Z, millennial, female, Black and Hispanic vote. Tafoya has more support from those aged 45 and older, as well as men and white likely voters. Both have 37 percent of the independent vote. The poll had a margin of error of 3 percent. The League of American Workers is not formally affiliated with the Republican Party, but it is a conservative advocacy organization led by former Trump adviser Steve Cortes. An August KSTP/SurveyUSA poll of 661 likely adults found Flanagan leading 46 percent to 41 percent, with about 11 percent undecided. The poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.3 percentage points. A Mason-Dixon Polling & Research survey, which did not poll specific candidates, found that Democrats lead Republicans on the generic ballot in the Senate race, 49 percent to 41 percent. It was sponsored by KARE-TV, the Minnesota Star Tribune and the University of Minnesota Hubbard School of Journalism and Mass Communications, surveying 800 likely voters June 8-10. Prediction markets have Flanagan as the clear favorite to win the seat. According to Kalshi on Friday, Flanagan has a 90.3 percent chance of winning to Tafoya's 9.7 percent chance. Polymarket showed a similar finding on Friday afternoon, with Flanagan having a 92 percent chance to Tafoya's 9 percent. Democrats' Chances of Flipping the Senate Democrats need to flip four Republican-held seats and hold all of their own to take control of the chamber, which Republicans currently control 53-47. Democrats argue that voter concerns about the economy, Trump's declining approval ratings and the war with Iran could create openings in several competitive state races. Despite Democratic optimism, Republicans contend that they will maintain their Senate majority and retain control of Congress. Nationally, 35 percent of voters approve of Trump's job performance while 59 percent disapprove as of Friday, leaving him underwater with a net approval rating of -24, according to Civiqs' rolling online tracking poll of registered voters. As of Wednesday, the survey had garnered around 129,000 responses since January 20, 2025, when Trump was inaugurated for a second term. Nate Silver’s Silver Bulletin’s averages show Democrats leading in four races for GOP-held Senate seats, putting the party within reach of the four it needs, but with little room for error. Its latest updated averages show Democrats ahead in Alaska, Georgia, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas. Republicans lead in Florida, Iowa and Kansas. The most competitive races in seats Democrats currently hold are in Georgia and Michigan, both of which narrowly backed Trump in the 2024 presidential election but backed President Joe Biden in 2020. Democrats view GOP-held seats in Maine, which backed former Harris by 7 points, and North Carolina, which backed Trump by 3 points, as their top flip opportunities. Prediction markets remain divided on which party will control the Senate after the midterms. As of Friday, Kalshi gave Republicans a 53 percent chance of winning control of the chamber, while Polymarket slightly favored Democrats, giving them a 53 percent chance of securing a Senate majority. Minnesota's in-person early voting period begins on October 16. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: Flanagan, a Democrat, leads in a new Minnesota U.S. Senate poll, but Republican Michele Tafoya remains within striking distance.

news.title: 9/11: Biden, Harris, Mamdani Pay Tribute
news.text:
Former United States President, Joe Biden, former Vice President, Kamala Harris and New York City Mayor, Zohran Mamdani have paid tributes to the victims and heroes of the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks as the United States marks the 25th anniversary of the tragedy.

Biden, in a statement, said 2,977 people were killed in the attacks, while thousands more have died in the years since from illnesses linked to the attacks.

“Twenty-five years ago today, we lost 2,977 souls and in the years since, thousands more to illnesses caused by the attack on our country,” Biden wrote.

He said he and his wife, Jill Biden, were remembering the families who continue to live with the loss, while honouring the firefighters and police officers who rushed into the World Trade Center towers and the Pentagon, passengers who fought back aboard the hijacked plane that crashed near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, and the generation that served in the aftermath of the attacks.

Biden said the enduring lesson of September 11 was the importance of unity during moments of vulnerability.

“Even now, we remember the greatest lesson of one of our nation’s darkest days: at our most vulnerable, unity is our most powerful strength,” he said.

He however pledged that the victims of the attacks would never be forgotten.

Similarly, Harris reflected on the 25th anniversary, saying a generation had grown up since the attacks but the responsibility to remember the victims remained unchanged.

“25 years have passed since September 11, 2001. A generation has grown up in the years since, but our responsibility to remember has not changed,” Harris wrote.

She said Americans continue to remember those who went to work on September 11, 2001, but never returned home, as well as the families who have carried their memories for the past 25 years.

Harris pledged that their stories would continue to be told and their lives honoured, while expressing gratitude for the heroism displayed on the day of the attacks.

Also, Mamdani, in his message marking the anniversary, said terrorists killed nearly 3,000 people 25 years ago, including 2,753 New Yorkers.

The New York mayor urged residents to remember not only the victims but also the first responders, office workers and strangers who ran towards danger to help others.

He described the compassion, resilience and bravery displayed during the tragedy as extraordinary, saying those qualities helped New York City through one of its darkest days.

“Today, New York remembers. We will Never Forget,” Mamdani said.

The September 11 attacks remain one of the defining tragedies in modern US history, with annual commemorations held across the country to honour those killed and recognise the first responders and others affected by the attacks.

news.title: With JD Vance seemingly ready to take the Trump mantle in 2028, Rubio admits he has no plans to run for president
news.text:
As Vice President JD Vance positioned himself as President Donald Trump’s natural successor at the Republican midterms convention Thursday night, his principal rival, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, ruled himself out of the running. 

Vance, 42, delivered a 40-minute address in the American Airlines Center in Dallas that “felt like a presidential nominating convention speech,” according to Reuters, in which he attacked Democrats, paid tribute to Charlie Kirk on the anniversary of his assassination and rebuked a heckler with a Mexican flag. 

The VP was met with chants of “48!” by the MAGA crowd, backing him to become the country’s 48th president, and was congratulated by the 47th afterward, who told reporters aboard Air Force One that his deputy had done “very well” and was a “very talented guy.”

Vance has since joined the four previous presidents – Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden – in New York City to observe the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks at Ground Zero, an event the incumbent ducked in order to be at the Pentagon. 

By contrast, Rubio, 55, was not present for the two-day event in Dallas. He spent the week touring South America instead, where he gave an interview to Colombia’s RCN where he was asked about his own ambitions for the White House. 

“I don’t know what the future holds, but I have no plans at this time,” he answered.

“I’m not a candidate for anything right now. And I’m 100 percent focused on my job, and I have to be because I have two jobs.” The secretary was alluding to his secondary role as Trump’s acting national security adviser.

An insider subsequently told NBC News that Rubio “loves being secretary of state and is really enjoying the job” and has no intention of running in 2028 but added: “If you asked him if he’s interested in 2032 or 2036, he would probably say sure.” 

As a Florida senator, Rubio did seek the Republican nomination in 2016, a contest in which he sparred nastily with Trump before suspending his campaign after losing his home state.

More recently, he enjoyed a brief bounce in popularity following January’s successful surprise operation to remove Nicolas Maduro from power in Venezuela, only to subsequently fade into the background as the president’s Iran war took center stage. 

For a while, it was reported that Trump enjoyed asking conservatives behind the scenes whether they preferred Vance or Rubio as his heir, pitting the two friends against each other, with the latter politely indicating he would not run as a challenger to the VP.

The president has not publicly endorsed either man, nor has Vance definitely said he intends to run – he could yet choose to opt out, given that his wife Usha Vance has just given birth to their fourth child and the likelihood of Democrats profiting from a sharp reaction against Trump, whose approval ratings are currently languishing in the low 30s.

However, in private, the president has reportedly told his party’s donors: “At the end of the day, we need to elect JD.” 

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Texas Sen. Ted Cruz are two more names that have recently been put forward, with Trump saying of the former in late August: “I think he’s doing a fantastic job, but it’s very early to talk about that.” 

On the opposite side of the aisle, Vance’s predecessor as vice president, Kamala Harris, has been mentioned as a Democratic nominee again, although she has so far refused to commit.

The betting markets meanwhile favor the likes of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, who made waves recently by teasing Trump over his relationship with his executive assistant Natalie Harp. 

Much will depend on November’s midterms, which the speakers at Trump’s convention attempted to make about immigration, crime and culture war issues, rather than the president’s unpopular war and affordability, two subjects on which voters have routinely expressed their dissatisfaction to pollsters.

Trump himself promised U.S. citizens $5,000 checks as a reward for the GOP hanging onto the House of Representatives and Senate – which some have called a bribe and pointed out would cost $1.3 trillion – and called on attendees to pledge their allegiance to his cause or “go to hell.”
news.summary: Vice President JD Vance cheered on by audience at GOP midterms convention as Secretary of State Marco Rubio appears to back away from White House challenge
news.author: Joe Sommerlad

news.title: (VIDEO) Trump Says 'We Will Never, Ever Forget' 9/11 Victims as America Marks a Quarter Century Since Attacks
news.text: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump told a Pentagon ceremony on Friday that the United States would "never, ever forget" the dead of Sept. 11, 2001, as the country marked 25 years since hijackers flew four airliners into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field."In 25 years, a generation has passed since the terror attacks," Trump said, reading from teleprompters at the Defense Department memorial for the 184 people killed when American Airlines Flight 77 struck the building. "Yet time has not dimmed the honour of that day our country came face-to-face with true evil."Nearly 3,000 people died that morning. About 2,700 were killed in New York when two planes hit the Twin Towers. Forty passengers and crew died on United Airlines Flight 93 after they fought the hijackers and the jet crashed near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Families, first responders and officials gathered at all three sites. In Lower Manhattan, bells and silences marked the times the South Tower fell (9:59 a.m.), Flight 93 went down (10:03 a.m.) and the North Tower collapsed (10:28 a.m.).Trump tied remembrance to current fighting. "We were all New Yorkers that day," he said. "But we're also all Americans." He praised troops "working right now to ensure the world's number one sponsor of terror, the Islamic Republic of Iran, will never, ever have a nuclear weapon.""Today we renew the sacred oath that we first swore in their names a quarter of a century ago," he said. "We will never, ever forget. That's why we fight today." On days like Sept. 11, he added, "we learn what a country is truly made of. We're learning right now what we're made of, and we have to be strong and we have to be smart."He closed by saying the attacks "reminded us of the terrible power of hate" and also showed "the power of the American spirit." "No one can ever prepare for a day like 9/11. But we can always choose to be the kind of nation the world saw in those days after," he said. "We can raise our children to know that their country is good, that their fathers are brave, and that our flag is a symbol of justice and freedom."Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who was in ROTC at Princeton when the planes hit, spoke first at the Pentagon and made the same link more bluntly. "Twenty-five years later, America is stronger than ever before," he said in remarks previewed in ceremony coverage. He described post-2001 wars as "a generation of sacrifice, of valor, selfless and steadfast." "Even if imperfect, those conflicts were our retribution," he said."There are still enemies who hate us," Hegseth said. "Every day, enemies plot to curb our power and kill our citizens, including from Islamic terrorists abroad and at home. But we are ever vigilant, especially this place." Of the campaign against Iran he said: "Over the past six months, we have laid waste to the world's most prolific state sponsor of terrorism. Our warriors have fought an Islamic theocracy that has wished us death for nearly half a century."Former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, national security adviser on the day of the attacks, recalled the first report as a possible accident. "I was at my desk at the White House that day when my executive assistant, a young army officer, told me that a plane had hit the World Trade Center. What a strange accident, I thought." After the second impact she was moved to a bunker and could not reach Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld after the Pentagon was hit."Behind every name that we recite, there is a story, a life that mattered, a future unfulfilled, a void, a vast empty space in the heart of a husband, a wife, a son, a daughter, a sibling, a colleague, or a friend," Rice said. "We come together today to say that they will never be forgotten, and to honour their memory."In New York, former President Bill Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris issued statements and Clinton attended the ceremony. Harris said a generation has grown up since the attacks "but our responsibility to remember has not changed." "We remember the people who went to work that morning and never came home, and we remember the families who have carried their memories every day since," she said. Clinton said the nightmare cannot be erased, "but we can support the people who have given and lost so much by treating one another with respect." He also noted those later sickened by toxic dust.The names of the dead were read again at the National September 11 Memorial, a ritual now older than many of the Americans who watched it. BBC correspondent Nada Tawfik reported that nearly a third of the country is too young to remember the day itself. Clouds blocked the "Way of Light" inside the Oculus transit hall, where two ceiling slits are designed to throw twin beams onto the floor between the first impact and the second collapse. An inscription there reads: "Here the Sun stands at 10:28 am on September 11, completing a wedge of light."John Ryan, a retired court officer who lost friends in the towers and the firehouses, sat across the street from the memorial and looked at empty sky. "It was the day that changed the world. The day that changed my life," he said. He remembered a Friday vigil that week: "That night, everybody stood still. All the cars stopped. Nobody moved. You know, Manhattan, they don't stop for anything."Rich Baktis, who was in high school on Long Island in 2001, said the aftermath — not the morning — is what he wants younger people to know. "Everybody came together, and everybody helped everybody," he said. That togetherness, he added, was the "best part that came out of that terrible day."Gunter Engels, visiting from Belgium, lost a former brother-in-law who worked in the towers and was never found. "The world has never been the same after 9/11," he said.At Shanksville, a white marble wall of names faces the flight path of Flight 93, whose passengers are credited with stopping a strike on Washington. The three ceremonies ran on the same clock they have used for a quarter century: impact, collapse, crash, silence. The political overlay was new. The names were not.
news.summary: President Donald Trump commemorated the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks at the Pentagon, as ceremonies across the United States honoured victims, survivors and first responders.
news.author: Anthony Will

news.title: Fast-Rising Jon Ossoff Might Have Just Killed His Chances At Higher Office
news.text:
Democrat Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff might have just killed his chances at higher office by agreeing to campaign with one of the most unpopular modern politicians and failed presidential candidates: Kamala Harris. 

Ossoff, who is running for reelection against Republican Mike Collins in November, has seen his star rise in 2026 after keeping a lower profile earlier in his first Senate term. Increasingly picking fights with the Trump administration, going viral online, and maintaining strong fundraising and polling numbers have led many Democrats to speculate that he might run in the 2028 presidential primary. (RELATED: Where Democrats Think They Can Flip The Senate: New Ad Money Shows The Map)

Ossoff has denied the rumors, saying he has “zero interest” and is more focused on his family and Georgia. But if the rumors happen to be true, and the senator is seriously considering a 2028 run, he may have just committed his first mistake in the long slog to power. 

Harris, a deeply unpopular vice president under Joe Biden, is now beginning to flex her political muscles again after her blowout loss to Donald Trump in 2024. Her first big test will be the midterms. She recently told Vox Media’s Megan Rapinoe that the upcoming elections “[are] full-time occupying my thoughts, my mind and my work.” 

 “I’m spending full time working on doing everything I can to help people restore some balance in our government, which is through the midterms, winning back Congress, the House and the Senate,” Harris said. 

One part of this reemergence into Democrat politics is to boost (or perhaps destroy) Ossoff’s Senate campaign. 

Spokespersons for both Harris and Ossoff have confirmed that the former VP will stump with Ossoff in Georgia next month and headline a fundraising dinner hosted by Fulton County Democrats in Atlanta. Ossoff’s campaign previously told Politico that they would welcome the chance to campaign with her. 

Tellingly, several Democrats running to flip seats in more rural, conservative states do not want to associate themselves with Harris. 

Rob Sand, an independent-minded Democrat running for governor of Iowa, bluntly said of Harris during an interview with Politico in August, “No thanks. Let’s move on. We need some new leadership.” He also flat-out said “nope” when asked whether he would want Harris or Biden to campaign with him. 

In Alaska, Democrat Senate candidate Mary Peltola is keeping her distance from Harris. After Harris’s political action committee sent a fundraising email, signed by Harris, describing Peltola as the best chance to flip Alaska, the campaign swiftly shot down the association. 

“Mary isn’t seeking endorsements from anyone from the Lower 48. Her focus is and always will be Alaska,” a spokesperson for Peltola told local NBC affiliate KTUU. “That’s why she’s proud to have the endorsement of [the American Federation of Government Employees], the Alaska [American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations], the Alaska [International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers] Local 1547 and more than 10,000 Alaskans who have signed up to volunteer with the campaign.”

One possible explanation for why Ossoff is taking a different approach than Peltola might have to do with Georgia’s high black population, particularly in Atlanta, and Harris’s popularity among black, high-school-educated voters (at least according to this poll from 2025). Another poll found that Harris had a big lead among black voters compared to other potential 2028 Democrat contenders.

But in a state like Georgia, it’s hard to imagine independents getting excited and motivated to vote because Ossoff is campaigning with Harris. Harder still to imagine a dissatisfied young person leaping at the prospect of a candidate backed by such an empty suit. 

Harris’s support does not seem like a boon. If anything, she represents heavy political baggage that could drag down Ossoff’s reelection hopes. And losing in November to Mike Collins might leave Ossoff on the sidelines in 2028.
news.summary: Did he just make a big mistake?
news.author: John Loftus
